notes.front: What is a blade station?
notes.back: A point along a propeller blade, numbered by its distance in inches from the centre of the hub.
notes.explanation: Stations let a blade be analysed as a series of segments, each shown as its own aerofoil cross-section.
notes.example: Like mile markers measured from the start of a road: the point 30 inches out from the hub centre is the 30-inch station.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Basic Propeller Principles”, PDF p. 289
notes.evidence: For purposes of analysis, a blade can be divided into segments that are located by station numbers in inches from the center of the blade hub.

notes.front: What is blade angle?
notes.back: The angle between the chord line of a blade section and the plane in which the propeller rotates.
notes.explanation: It is usually given in degrees, and the blade's chord line is found much as a wing aerofoil's is.
notes.example: Like the tilt of a stair tread against the floor, but measured between the blade's chord and its plane of spin.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Basic Propeller Principles”, PDF p. 289
notes.evidence: Blade angle, usually measured in degrees, is the angle between the chordline of the blade and the plane of rotation. The chordline of the propeller blade is determined in about the same manner as the chordline of an airfoil.

notes.front: What is geometric pitch?
notes.back: The distance a propeller should advance in one revolution if there were no slippage.
notes.explanation: It is a theoretical distance; effective pitch is how far the propeller actually advances in air.
notes.example: Like the distance a screw moves into wood in one turn, except that air lets a propeller slip back a little.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Aerodynamic Process”, PDF p. 288
notes.evidence: Geometric pitch is the distance a propeller should advance in one revolution with no slippage; effective pitch is the distance it actually advances.

notes.front: What is blade twist, also called pitch distribution?
notes.back: The twist in a propeller blade from the shank to the tip.
notes.explanation: Each section of the blade travels at a different speed, the tip much faster than the inner part.
notes.example: Like a ribbon given a gradual half-turn along its length: the blade's angle changes steadily from root to tip.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Aerodynamic Factors”, PDF p. 291
notes.evidence: Pitch distribution is the twist in the blade from the shank to the blade tip, due to the variation in speeds that each section of the blade is traveling. The tip of the blade is traveling much faster than the inner portion of the blade.

notes.front: What is centrifugal twisting moment?
notes.back: The twisting effect of centrifugal force on a spinning blade that tends to turn it towards a low blade angle.
notes.explanation: It is the stronger of the two twisting forces on a rotating blade.
notes.example: Like a spinning skater's arms being pulled flat by the spin, the blade is pulled towards a flatter angle.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Basic Propeller Principles”, PDF p. 289
notes.evidence: Centrifugal twisting force, being greater than the aerodynamic twisting force, tends to force the blades toward a low blade angle.

notes.front: What is aerodynamic twisting moment?
notes.back: The aerodynamic force on a rotating blade that tends to turn it towards a high blade angle.
notes.explanation: It works against centrifugal twisting, which is the greater of the two.
notes.example: Like a weathervane being nudged round by the air, the blade is nudged towards a steeper angle.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Basic Propeller Principles”, PDF p. 289
notes.evidence: Aerodynamic twisting force tends to turn the blades to a high blade angle. [Figure 7-8D] Centrifugal twisting force, being greater than the aerodynamic twisting force, tends to force the blades toward a low blade angle.

notes.front: What is a fixed-pitch propeller?
notes.back: A propeller whose blade angle is built in and cannot be changed after it is made.
notes.explanation: Nothing on the aircraft can move the blades; the angle was set when the propeller was built.
notes.example: Like a one-speed bicycle: simple and cheap, but geared for one pace.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Fixed-Pitch Propeller”, PDF p. 292
notes.evidence: As the name implies, a fixed-pitch propeller has the blade pitch, or blade angle, built into the propeller. [Figure 7-11] The blade angle cannot be changed after the propeller is built.

notes.front: What is a test club?
notes.back: A multi-blade propeller used to test and break in reciprocating engines.
notes.explanation: It is made to put the correct load on the engine during the break-in period.
notes.example: Like the brake on an engine test bench, but it loads the engine by pushing air.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Test Club Propeller”, PDF p. 292
notes.evidence: A test club is used to test and break in reciprocating engines. [Figure 7-12] They are made to provide the correct amount of load on the engine during the test break-in period.

notes.front: What is a ground-adjustable propeller?
notes.back: A propeller whose blade angle can be changed only when it is not turning, by loosening the blade clamps.
notes.explanation: Once clamped, it behaves in flight exactly like a fixed-pitch propeller.
notes.example: Like an adjustable spanner: you set the jaws first, then they stay put while you work.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Ground-Adjustable Propeller”, PDF p. 292
notes.evidence: The ground-adjustable propeller operates as a fixed-pitch propeller. The pitch, or blade angle, can be changed only when the propeller is not turning. This is done by loosening the clamping mechanism that holds the blades in place.

notes.front: What is a controllable-pitch propeller?
notes.back: A propeller whose blade angle the pilot can change in flight, directly, while it rotates.
notes.explanation: The blade angle then stays where it is until the pilot changes it again.
notes.example: Like a manual gearbox: the driver picks each gear and it stays there until changed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Controllable-Pitch Propeller”, PDF p. 293
notes.evidence: With the controllable-pitch type, the blade angle can be changed in flight, but the pilot must change the propeller blade angle directly. The blade angle will not change again until the pilot changes it.

notes.front: What is a constant-speed propeller?
notes.back: A governor-controlled propeller that changes its blade angle automatically to keep engine rpm constant.
notes.explanation: The blade angle follows the governor rather than direct pilot input, so rpm holds steady as conditions change.
notes.example: Like cruise control in a car, but it holds engine speed by changing the propeller's bite on the air.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Controllable-Pitch Propeller”, PDF p. 293
notes.evidence: The governor-controlled, constant-speed propeller changes the blade angle automatically, keeping engine rpm constant.

notes.front: What does a propeller governor do in a constant-speed system?
notes.back: It senses engine rpm and sends oil under pressure to the propeller cylinder, or releases it, to change blade angle.
notes.explanation: The change in oil volume in the cylinder changes the blade angle and so holds the system rpm.
notes.example: Like a thermostat that switches heating on and off, but it senses rpm and moves oil.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Governor”, PDF p. 294
notes.evidence: In a constant-speed propeller system, the governor responds to a change in engine rpm by directing oil under pressure to the propeller hydraulic cylinder or by releasing oil from the hydraulic cylinder.

notes.front: What is the propeller control on a constant-speed installation?
notes.back: The flight-deck lever, full forward for increase rpm and aft for decrease rpm, that sets the governor speeder-spring tension.
notes.explanation: It works through the governor rather than moving the blades directly.
notes.example: Like the dial on a thermostat: it sets the target, and the governor does the work.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Controls & Instruments”, PDF p. 291
notes.evidence: The two positions for the control are increase rpm (full forward) and decrease rpm (pulled aft). This control is directly connected to the propeller governor and, by moving the control, adjusts the tension on the governor speeder spring.

notes.front: What is an underspeed condition of a propeller governor?
notes.back: The engine is running below the rpm set by the pilot, and the governor flyweights tilt inward.
notes.explanation: There is too little centrifugal force on the flyweights to overcome the speeder spring.
notes.example: Like a car slowing on a hill below its cruise-control setting.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Underspeed Condition”, PDF p. 295
notes.evidence: When the engine is operating below the rpm set by the pilot using the flight deck control, the governor is operating in an underspeed condition. [Figure 7-17] In this condition, the flyweights tilt inward because there is not enough centrifugal force on the flyweights to overcome the force of the speeder spring.

notes.front: What is an overspeed condition of a propeller governor?
notes.back: The engine is running above the rpm set by the pilot, and the governor flyweights tilt outward.
notes.explanation: Centrifugal force on the flyweights is greater than the speeder spring force.
notes.example: Like a car running downhill faster than its cruise-control setting.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Overspeed Condition”, PDF p. 297
notes.evidence: When the engine is operating above the rpm set by the pilot using the flight deck control, the governor is operating in an overspeed condition. [Figure 7-18] In an overspeed condition, the centrifugal force acting on the flyweights is greater than the speeder spring force. The flyweights tilt outward and raise the pilot valve.

notes.front: What is an on-speed condition of a propeller governor?
notes.back: The engine is at the set rpm: flyweight force balances the speeder spring, and no oil moves to or from the propeller.
notes.explanation: With the pilot valve centred, oil is neither sent to nor drained from the propeller cylinder.
notes.example: Like a car holding exactly its cruise-control speed on a level road.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “On-Speed Condition”, PDF p. 297
notes.evidence: When the engine is operating at the rpm set by the pilot using the flight deck control, the governor is operating on speed. [Figure 7-19] In an on-speed condition, the centrifugal force acting on the flyweights is balanced by the speeder spring, and the pilot valve is neither directing oil to nor from the propeller hydraulic cylinder.

notes.front: What is a feathering propeller?
notes.back: A constant-speed propeller for multi-engine aircraft that can turn its blades to about 90°.
notes.explanation: It is usually feathered when its engine fails to develop power to turn the propeller.
notes.example: Like turning an oar edge-on so it slices through the water instead of pulling.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Feathering Propellers”, PDF p. 294
notes.evidence: A feathering propeller is a constant-speed propeller used on multi-engine aircraft that has a mechanism to change the pitch to an angle of approximately 90°. A propeller is usually feathered when the engine fails to develop power to turn the propeller.

notes.front: What is a reverse-pitch propeller?
notes.back: A controllable propeller whose blades can be moved to a negative angle, giving thrust opposite to normal.
notes.explanation: The negative blade angle turns the direction of thrust round.
notes.example: Like putting a boat's propeller astern to stop at the quay.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Reverse-Pitch Propellers”, PDF p. 294
notes.evidence: The purpose of the reversible pitch feature is to produce a negative blade angle that produces thrust opposite the normal forward direction.

notes.front: How is a wooden propeller built?
notes.back: From separate glued layers of carefully selected, well-seasoned hardwood, not from one solid block.
notes.explanation: The laminations are chosen and seasoned before they are glued and shaped.
notes.example: Like plywood or a laminated beam, but carved into a blade.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Fixed-Pitch Wooden Propellers”, PDF p. 298
notes.evidence: A wooden propeller is not constructed from a solid block but is built up of a number of separate layers of carefully selected and well-seasoned hardwoods.

notes.front: What is a metal fixed-pitch propeller?
notes.back: A fixed-pitch propeller of metal that looks like a wooden one, except its sections are usually thinner.
notes.explanation: Side by side the two look alike; the thinner sections are the usual giveaway.
notes.example: Like a wooden propeller's twin cast in metal, but slimmer.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Metal Fixed-Pitch Propellers”, PDF p. 299
notes.evidence: Metal fixed-pitch propellers are similar in general appearance to a wooden propeller, except that the sections are usually thinner.

notes.front: What is an unfeathering accumulator?
notes.back: A store connected to the governor that traps an air-oil charge when the propeller feathers and releases it to unfeather.
notes.explanation: It unfeathers in a very short time and starts the engine windmilling, which is why training aircraft use it.
notes.example: Like a spring-loaded door closer: energy stored earlier does the job later without a pump.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Unfeathering”, PDF p. 302
notes.evidence: Provide an accumulator connected to the governor with a valve to trap an air-oil charge when the propeller is feathered but released to the propeller when the rpm control is returned to normal position. This system is used with training aircraft because it unfeathers the propeller in a very short time and starts the engine windmilling.

notes.front: What is a slinger ring?
notes.back: A circular U-shaped channel on the rear of the propeller that receives anti-icing fluid from a fixed nozzle.
notes.explanation: Centrifugal force then carries the fluid through nozzles to each blade shank.
notes.example: Like a spinning gutter fed from a fixed tap, flinging the fluid outward along the blades.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Anti-Icing Systems”, PDF p. 303
notes.evidence: Fluid is transferred from a stationary nozzle on the engine nose case into a circular U-shaped channel (slinger ring) mounted on the rear of the propeller assembly. The fluid under pressure of centrifugal force is transferred through nozzles to each blade shank.

notes.front: What is a propeller deicing boot?
notes.back: A boot with internal heating elements, bonded with adhesive to each blade's leading edge.
notes.explanation: It sits on the leading edge, where it is fixed, and carries its own heating elements.
notes.example: Like a heated rear window on a car, but a strip on each blade's leading edge.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Deicing Systems”, PDF p. 304
notes.evidence: A deice boot contains internal heating elements or dual elements. [Figure 7-30] The boot is securely attached to the leading edge of each blade with adhesive.

notes.front: What is synchrophasing?
notes.back: Keeping a preset angular relationship between a master propeller's blades and those of the slave propellers.
notes.explanation: Matching rpm and blade phase between the left and right propellers reduces cabin noise.
notes.example: Like rowers keeping their oars in the same part of the stroke, not just at the same pace.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Synchronization & Synchrophasing”, PDF p. 305
notes.evidence: The synchrophasing system is designed to maintain a preset angular relationship between the designated master propeller and the slave propellers. A typical synchrophasing system is an electronic system. [Figure 7-31] It functions to match the rpm of both engines and establish a blade phase relationship between the left and right propellers to reduce cabin noise.

notes.front: What is an autofeather system?
notes.back: A system that feathers a propeller automatically if power is lost from either engine, normally used only for takeoff, approach and landing.
notes.explanation: It acts on its own in the phases of flight where it is armed.
notes.example: Like a circuit breaker that trips on a fault without anyone touching it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Autofeathering System”, PDF p. 306
notes.evidence: An autofeather system is used normally only during takeoff, approach, and landing. It is used to feather the propeller automatically if power is lost from either engine.

notes.front: What is blade tracking?
notes.back: Finding the positions of the blade tips relative to each other, to see that they turn in the same plane.
notes.explanation: It shows only where the blades are relative to one another, not their actual path.
notes.example: Like checking that every spoke of a wheel lines up, but for propeller tips.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Blade Tracking”, PDF p. 308
notes.evidence: Blade tracking is the process of determining the positions of the tips of the propeller blades relative to each other (blades rotating in the same plane of rotation). Tracking shows only the relative position of the blades, not their actual path.

notes.front: What is a universal propeller protractor used for?
notes.back: Checking blade angles, with the propeller on a balancing stand or installed on the engine.
notes.explanation: It works in both places, so the propeller need not come off the engine to be measured.
notes.example: Like a carpenter's angle finder, but zeroed on the propeller's plane of rotation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Universal Propeller Protractor”, PDF p. 309
notes.evidence: The universal propeller protractor can be used to check propeller blade angles when the propeller is on a balancing stand or installed on the aircraft engine.

notes.front: What does static balancing correct?
notes.back: Static imbalance: a propeller whose centre of gravity does not lie on its axis of rotation.
notes.explanation: Unbalance of either kind is a source of vibration in an aircraft.
notes.example: Like balancing a bicycle wheel so it stays put at any position when spun gently and let go.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Balancing”, PDF p. 310
notes.evidence: Propeller unbalance, which is a source of vibration in an aircraft, may be either static or dynamic. Propeller static imbalance occurs when the center of gravity (CG) of the propeller does not coincide with the axis of rotation.

notes.front: What is dynamic balancing of a propeller?
notes.back: Spin balancing with an analyser kit to reduce vibration of the propeller and spinner assembly.
notes.explanation: It is done with the propeller spinning, which is why it is also called spin balancing.
notes.example: Like wheel balancing on a spinning machine at a tyre shop, but done on the aircraft.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Dynamic Balancing”, PDF p. 311
notes.evidence: Propellers can also be dynamically balanced (spin balanced) with an analyzer kit to reduce the vibration levels of the propeller and spinner assembly.

notes.front: What is hunting in a propeller system?
notes.back: A cyclic variation in engine speed above and below the desired speed.
notes.explanation: The variation is a cycle: speed keeps swinging either side of the setting.
notes.example: Like a shower whose temperature keeps swinging hot and cold around the setting.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Hunting & Surging”, PDF p. 316
notes.evidence: Hunting is characterized by a cyclic variation in engine speed above and below desired speed.

notes.front: What is turboprop propeller control?
notes.back: The fuel control and propeller governor working together to set rpm, fuel flow and blade angle.
notes.explanation: The two units act as a pair, so the thrust needed for the desired power comes from all three settings together.
notes.example: Like a car's engine management and automatic gearbox agreeing on revs and gear.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Turboprop Engines & Propeller Control Systems”, PDF p. 317
notes.evidence: The fuel control and the propeller governor together establish the correct combination of rpm, fuel flow, and propeller blade angle to create sufficient propeller thrust to provide the desired power.

notes.front: What is a turboprop reduction gear assembly for?
notes.back: It cuts the engine's high rpm to a propeller rpm that stays below the maximum propeller tip speed.
notes.explanation: The maximum tip speed is the speed of sound.
notes.example: Like a low gear on a bicycle, but turning a fast turbine into a slower propeller.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Reduction Gear Assembly”, PDF p. 317
notes.evidence: The function of the reduction gear assembly is to reduce the high rpm from the engine to a propeller rpm that can be maintained without exceeding the maximum propeller tip speed (speed of sound).

notes.front: What is the beta range of a turboprop?
notes.back: The ground-handling range below flight idle, where the power lever, not the governor, sets blade angle.
notes.explanation: Below flight idle the normal rpm and blade-angle schedule can no longer handle the engine efficiently.
notes.example: Like shifting a car into manual low gear for parking, where you control it directly instead of the automatic.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Turboprop Engines & Propeller Control Systems”, PDF p. 317
notes.evidence: Below the “flight idle” power lever position, the coordinated rpm blade angle schedule becomes incapable of handling the engine efficiently. Here, the ground handling range, referred to as the beta range, is encountered. In the beta range of the throttle quadrant, the propeller blade angle is not governed by the propeller governor but is controlled by the power lever position.

notes.front: What does the beta valve do in the Hartzell turboprop propeller system?
notes.back: Moved forward by the beta linkage, it stops oil to the propeller so blades go no lower than the minimum flight angle.
notes.explanation: Stopping the oil stops the blades at the primary blade angle, the lowest allowed in flight.
notes.example: Like the float valve in a cistern that shuts the supply once the level is reached.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Pratt & Whitney PT6 Hartzell Propeller System”, PDF p. 318
notes.evidence: Forward movement of the beta valve stops the oil supply to the propeller. This prevents the blade angles from going any lower. This is the primary blade angle (PBA) and is the minimum blade angle allowed for flight operation.

notes.front: What is the Hamilton Standard Hydromatic propeller?
notes.back: A double-acting propeller in which engine oil pressure on one side of the piston opposes governor oil pressure on the other.
notes.explanation: The two opposing hydraulic forces are what change and control the blade angle.
notes.example: Like a tug-of-war between two hoses pushing on either side of one piston.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Hamilton Standard Hydromatic Propellers”, PDF p. 320
notes.evidence: This propeller system is a double-acting hydraulic propeller system in which the hydraulic pressure (engine oil pressure) on one piston dome is used against governor oil pressure on the other side of the piston. These two opposing hydraulic forces are used to control and change blade angle or pitch.

notes.front: Which part of a propeller blade is the thick, rounded portion near the hub?
notes.back: The blade shank.
notes.explanation: Its thickness is there to give the blade strength.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Basic Propeller Principles”, PDF p. 289
notes.evidence: The blade shank is the thick, rounded portion of the propeller blade near the hub and is designed to give strength to the blade.

notes.front: Which side of a propeller blade is the blade back, and which the blade face?
notes.back: The back is the cambered, curved side; the face is the flat side.
notes.explanation: The back is compared with the upper surface of a wing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Basic Propeller Principles”, PDF p. 289
notes.evidence: The blade back is the cambered or curved side of the blade, similar to the upper surface of an aircraft wing. The blade face is the flat side of the propeller blade.

notes.front: What is propeller slip?
notes.back: The difference between the geometric pitch and the effective pitch.
notes.explanation: Geometric pitch assumes no slippage; effective pitch is what the propeller actually advances in air.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Aerodynamic Process”, PDF p. 288
notes.evidence: Propeller slip is the difference between the geometric pitch of the propeller and its effective pitch.

notes.front: How is geometric pitch usually calculated, in pitch inches?
notes.back: 2 × π × R × tangent of the blade angle at the 75 percent station, where R is the radius there.
notes.explanation: The blade angle used is the one at the 75 percent station, not at the tip or the hub.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Aerodynamic Process”, PDF p. 288
notes.evidence: Geometric pitch is usually expressed in pitch inches and calculated by using the following formula: GP = 2 x π x R x tangent of blade angle at 75 percent station

notes.front: Are pitch and blade angle the same thing?
notes.back: No, but pitch is largely determined by blade angle, so the terms are often used interchangeably.
notes.explanation: An increase or decrease in one usually goes with an increase or decrease in the other.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Aerodynamic Process”, PDF p. 288
notes.evidence: Pitch is not the same as blade angle, but because pitch is largely determined by blade angle, the two terms are often used interchangeably. An increase or decrease in one is usually associated with an increase or decrease in the other.

notes.front: Lift-versus-drag curves show that the most efficient propeller angle of attack is a small one, from {{c1::2° to 4°}} positive.
notes.explanation: The same kind of curve is drawn for wings, because a blade section is an aerofoil.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Aerodynamic Factors”, PDF p. 291
notes.evidence: Lift versus drag curves, which are drawn for propellers as well as wings, indicate that the most efficient AOA is a small one varying from 2° to 4° positive.

notes.front: Roughly what speed are propeller-driven aircraft limited to, and why?
notes.back: About 400 mph, because propeller speed itself is limited.
notes.explanation: Too high a tip speed brings poor efficiency, flutter and vibration.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “General”, PDF p. 287
notes.evidence: Excessive blade tip speed (rotating the propeller too fast) may result not only in poor blade efficiency, but also in fluttering and vibration. Since the propeller speed is limited, the aircraft speed of a propeller driven aircraft is also limited—to approximately 400 miles per hour (mph).

notes.front: Which force on a rotating propeller is the most dominant?
notes.back: Centrifugal force, which tends to throw the blades away from the hub.
notes.explanation: It pulls outward along the blade rather than bending or twisting it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Basic Propeller Principles”, PDF p. 289
notes.evidence: Centrifugal force is a physical force that tends to throw the rotating propeller blades away from the hub. [Figure 7-8A] This is the most dominant force on the propeller.

notes.front: Which way does torque bending force bend the blades?
notes.back: Opposite to the direction of rotation.
notes.explanation: It comes from air resistance to the blades as they turn.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Basic Propeller Principles”, PDF p. 289
notes.evidence: Torque bending force, in the form of air resistance, tends to bend the propeller blades in the direction opposite that of rotation.

notes.front: Which way does thrust bending force bend the blades?
notes.back: Forward, as the aircraft is pulled through the air.
notes.explanation: It is the thrust load itself acting on the blades.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Basic Propeller Principles”, PDF p. 289
notes.evidence: Thrust bending force is the thrust load that tends to bend propeller blades forward as the aircraft is pulled through the air.

notes.front: What is propeller flutter?
notes.back: Vibration in which the blade ends twist back and forth at high frequency about an axis perpendicular to the crankshaft.
notes.explanation: A propeller must be rigid enough to prevent it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Basic Propeller Principles”, PDF p. 290
notes.evidence: A propeller must also be rigid enough to prevent fluttering, a type of vibration in which the ends of the blade twist back and forth at high frequency around an axis perpendicular to the engine crankshaft.

notes.front: On a controllable-pitch propeller, which twisting force is sometimes used to move blades to low pitch, and which to high pitch?
notes.back: Centrifugal twisting to low pitch; aerodynamic twisting to high pitch.
notes.explanation: At least two of the forces on the blades are put to work moving them.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Basic Propeller Principles”, PDF p. 289
notes.evidence: At least two of these forces acting on the propellers blades are used to move the blades on a controllable pitch propeller. Centrifugal twisting force is sometimes used to move the blades to the low pitch position, while aerodynamic twisting force is used to move the blades into high pitch.

notes.front: On the constant-speed feathering propeller described, how large is blade aerodynamic twisting force?
notes.back: Usually very small compared with the other forces, and it can act to increase or decrease blade angle.
notes.explanation: 'Usually' and 'can' matter: it is minor, and its direction is not fixed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Constant-Speed Feathering Propeller”, PDF p. 301
notes.evidence: Blade aerodynamic twisting force is usually very small in relation to the other forces and can attempt to increase or decrease blade angle.

notes.front: Where is a tractor propeller mounted?
notes.back: On the upstream end of a drive shaft, in front of the supporting structure.
notes.explanation: Most aircraft use this arrangement.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Tractor Propeller”, PDF p. 291
notes.evidence: Tractor propellers are those mounted on the upstream end of a drive shaft in front of the supporting structure. Most aircraft are equipped with this type of propeller.

notes.front: Which are the simplest types of propeller?
notes.back: The fixed-pitch and the ground-adjustable propeller.
notes.explanation: Complexity rises from these to controllable-pitch and then constant-speed systems.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Types of Propellers”, PDF p. 292
notes.evidence: There are various types or classes of propellers, the simplest of which are the fixed-pitch and ground-adjustable propellers. The complexity of propeller systems increases from these simpler forms to controllable-pitch and complex constantspeed systems (automatic systems).

notes.front: On what aircraft is a fixed-pitch propeller used, and what are its advantages?
notes.back: Aircraft of low power, speed, range or altitude; it costs less and is simple to operate.
notes.explanation: Many single-engine aircraft use it for those reasons.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Fixed-Pitch Propeller”, PDF p. 292
notes.evidence: The fixed-pitch propeller is used on aircraft of low power, speed, range, or altitude. Many singleengine aircraft use fixed-pitch propellers and the advantages of these are less expense and their simple operation.

notes.front: Why does any change in flight conditions reduce a fixed-pitch propeller's efficiency?
notes.back: It is designed for best efficiency at one rotational and forward speed.
notes.explanation: It fits one set of aircraft and engine speeds; away from them, both propeller and engine lose efficiency.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Fixed-Pitch Propeller”, PDF p. 292
notes.evidence: Fixed-pitch propellers are designed for best efficiency at one rotational and forward speed. They are designed to fit a set of conditions of both aircraft and engine speeds and any change in these conditions reduces the efficiency of both the propeller and the engine.

notes.front: An aircraft with a constant-speed propeller enters a climb at an unchanged throttle. What does the blade angle do?
notes.back: It decreases just enough to stop engine speed falling.
notes.explanation: Holding rpm this way lets the engine keep its power output at the same throttle.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Constant-Speed Propellers”, PDF p. 293
notes.evidence: When the aircraft goes into a climb, the blade angle of the propeller decreases just enough to prevent the engine speed from decreasing. The engine can maintain its power output if the throttle setting is not changed.

notes.front: What does the tension of the governor speeder spring set?
notes.back: The maximum engine rpm in the governor mode.
notes.explanation: The pilot adjusts that tension with the propeller control.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Governor”, PDF p. 295
notes.evidence: The tension on this spring can be adjusted by the propeller control on the control quadrant. The tension of the speeder spring sets the maximum rpm of the engine in the governor mode.

notes.front: In a single-acting propeller governor, what raises the engine oil pressure, and what controls the pilot valve?
notes.back: A gear pump raises the pressure; flyweights control the pilot valve.
notes.explanation: The governor takes oil from the lubricating system and boosts it for the pitch change.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Governor Mechanism”, PDF p. 295
notes.evidence: It consists of a gear pump to increase the pressure of the engine oil, a pilot valve controlled by flyweights in the governor to

notes.front: In an underspeed condition, what does the pilot valve do to propeller pitch?
notes.back: Forced down by the speeder spring, it meters oil to decrease pitch and raise rpm.
notes.explanation: Lower pitch takes load off the engine, so it speeds back up.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Underspeed Condition”, PDF p. 295
notes.evidence: The pilot valve, forced down by the speeder spring, meters oil flow to decrease propeller pitch and raise engine rpm.

notes.front: In an overspeed condition, what does the pilot valve do to propeller pitch?
notes.back: Raised by the flyweights, it meters oil to increase pitch and lower rpm.
notes.explanation: Higher pitch adds load, slowing the engine back to the set rpm.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Overspeed Condition”, PDF p. 297
notes.evidence: The flyweights tilt outward and raise the pilot valve. The pilot valve then meters oil flow to increase propeller pitch and lower engine rpm.

notes.front: The speeder spring propeller governing range is limited to about {{c1::200 rpm}}.
notes.explanation: Beyond that range the governor cannot hold the correct rpm.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “On-Speed Condition”, PDF p. 297
notes.evidence: The speeder spring propeller governing range is limited to about 200 rpm. Beyond this rpm, the governor cannot maintain the correct rpm.

notes.front: What holds feathered blades in feather?
notes.back: Aerodynamic forces.
notes.explanation: With the blades parallel to the airstream the propeller stops, with little or no windmilling.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Feathering Propellers”, PDF p. 294
notes.evidence: With the blades parallel to the airstream, the propeller stops turning and minimum windmilling, if any, occurs. The blades are held in feather by aerodynamic forces.

notes.front: On almost all small feathering propellers, what drives the blades to low pitch, and what to high pitch?
notes.back: Oil pressure to low pitch; blade flyweights, springs and compressed air to high pitch.
notes.explanation: 'Almost all' is the handbook's hedge: a few designs differ.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Feathering Propellers”, PDF p. 294
notes.evidence: Almost all small feathering propellers use oil pressure to take the propeller to low pitch and blade flyweights, springs, and compressed air to take the blades to high pitch.

notes.front: Why do small feathering propellers have latches that lock the blades in low pitch at shutdown?
notes.back: Feathered blades at the next start would put an undue load on the engine.
notes.explanation: Without the latches the blades would go to feather as the propeller slows at shutdown.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Feathering Propellers”, PDF p. 294
notes.evidence: Latches are needed to prevent excess load on the engine at start up. If the blade were in the feathered position during engine start, the engine would be placed under an undue load during a time when the engine is already subject to wear.

notes.front: On the Hartzell-type feathering system described, an elapsed time for feathering of between {{c1::3 and 10 seconds}} is usual.
notes.explanation: A larger passage through the governor and a heavier spring make it quicker.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Constant-Speed Feathering Propeller”, PDF p. 302
notes.evidence: The larger the passage is through the governor and the heavier the spring, the quicker the feathering action is. An elapsed time for feathering of between 3 and 10 seconds is usual with this system.

notes.front: After touchdown, what are two benefits of reversing the propellers?
notes.back: A shorter ground roll and less brake wear.
notes.explanation: Reverse thrust brakes the aircraft aerodynamically.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Reverse-Pitch Propellers”, PDF p. 294
notes.evidence: This aerodynamically brakes the aircraft and reduces ground roll after landing. Reversing the propellers also reduces aircraft speed quickly on the runway just after touchdown and minimizes aircraft brake wear.

notes.front: What is the normal sequence of blade travel from feather to reverse?
notes.back: Feather, high pitch, low pitch, locks or ground idle, reverse pitch, then back along the same path.
notes.explanation: The blades pass through every position in order both ways; none is skipped.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Figure 7-3, Propeller range positions”, PDF p. 288
notes.evidence: Normal sequence of blade travel is feather, high pitch, low pitch, locks/ground idle, reverse pitch, and then back following the same path.

image.alt: Bar chart of typical propeller blade angles: feather 85 to 90 degrees, power 20 to 35, flight idle 10 to 12, locks 1 to 2, ground idle 0, reverse minus 2 to minus 8 degrees. Normal travel runs feather, high pitch, low pitch, locks or ground idle, reverse, then back the same way.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from FAA-H-8083-32B, Figure 7-3

notes.front: In the handbook's typical propeller blade positions, what is the blade angle at feather?
notes.explanation: Feather is the highest angle in the range and the first in the normal travel sequence.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Figure 7-3, Propeller range positions”, PDF p. 288
notes.evidence: Feather Power 85 to 90° 20 to 35°

notes.front: In the handbook's typical propeller blade positions, what is the blade angle range for power?
notes.explanation: Power sits between feather and flight idle in the travel sequence.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Figure 7-3, Propeller range positions”, PDF p. 288
notes.evidence: Feather Power 85 to 90° 20 to 35°

notes.front: In the handbook's typical propeller blade positions, what is the blade angle at flight idle?
notes.explanation: Flight idle is the lowest angle used in flight in this range, above the locks.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Figure 7-3, Propeller range positions”, PDF p. 288
notes.evidence: Flight idle 10 to 12° Locks 1 to 2°

notes.front: In the handbook's typical propeller blade positions, what is the blade angle on the locks?
notes.explanation: The locks sit just above ground idle, near flat pitch.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Figure 7-3, Propeller range positions”, PDF p. 288
notes.evidence: Flight idle 10 to 12° Locks 1 to 2°

notes.front: In the handbook's typical propeller blade positions, what is the blade angle at ground idle?
notes.explanation: Zero blade angle comes between the locks and reverse.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Figure 7-3, Propeller range positions”, PDF p. 288
notes.evidence: Ground idle Reverse 0° −2 to −8°

notes.front: In the handbook's typical propeller blade positions, what is the blade angle range in reverse?
notes.explanation: Reverse is the only range with negative blade angles.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Figure 7-3, Propeller range positions”, PDF p. 288
notes.evidence: Ground idle Reverse 0° −2 to −8°

notes.front: Which wood is most widely used for wooden propellers?
notes.back: Birch.
notes.explanation: Other hardwoods such as mahogany, cherry, black walnut and oak are used to some extent.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Fixed-Pitch Wooden Propellers”, PDF p. 298
notes.evidence: Many woods, such as mahogany, cherry, black walnut, and oak, are used to some extent, but birch is the most widely used.

notes.front: Why must the small holes near the tip of a wooden blade's metal tipping be kept open?
notes.back: They let moisture that condenses between metal and wood drain away or be thrown out.
notes.explanation: Centrifugal force helps throw the moisture out through them.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Fixed-Pitch Wooden Propellers”, PDF p. 299
notes.evidence: Since moisture condenses on the tipping between the metal and the wood, the tipping is provided with small holes near the blade tip to allow this moisture to drain away or be thrown out by centrifugal force. It is important that these drain holes be kept open at all times.

notes.front: Why did early one-piece forged Duralumin propellers cost less to maintain than wooden ones?
notes.back: They were made in one piece.
notes.explanation: They were also lighter, because blade-clamping devices were eliminated.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Metal Fixed-Pitch Propellers”, PDF p. 299
notes.evidence: Compared to wooden propellers, they were lighter in weight because of elimination of blade-clamping devices, offered a lower maintenance cost because they were made in one piece,

notes.front: On most Hartzell aluminium and steel hub models, what increases pitch, and what gives low pitch?
notes.back: Centrifugal force on blade flyweights increases pitch; governor oil pressure gives low pitch.
notes.explanation: This is the usual arrangement; one nonfeathering model is the exception.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Hartzell Constant-Speed, Nonfeathering”, PDF p. 300
notes.evidence: Most of the Hartzell propeller aluminum and steel hub models use centrifugal force acting on blade flyweights to increase blade pitch and governor oil pressure for low pitch.

notes.front: What does ice on a propeller blade do? Name two effects.
notes.back: It distorts the aerofoil, losing efficiency, and generally causes unbalance and destructive vibration.
notes.explanation: Ice generally collects asymmetrically, which is where the unbalance comes from; it also adds weight.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Ice Control Systems”, PDF p. 303
notes.evidence: Ice formation on a propeller blade, in effect, produces a distorted blade airfoil section that causes a loss in propeller efficiency. Generally, ice collects asymmetrically on a propeller blade and produces propeller unbalance and destructive vibration and increases the weight of the blades.

notes.front: How far along the blade do anti-icing feed shoes extend?
notes.back: From the blade shank to about the 75 percent radius station.
notes.explanation: They are narrow rubber strips with open channels for the fluid.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Anti-Icing Systems”, PDF p. 303
notes.evidence: These feed shoes are a narrow strip of rubber extending from the blade shank to a blade station that is approximately 75 percent of the propeller radius.

notes.front: In propeller electric deicing, how is power passed from the engine to the rotating propeller?
notes.back: A brush block on the engine feeds a slip ring that turns with the propeller.
notes.explanation: The slip ring gives the current path to the blade deice boots.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Deicing Systems”, PDF p. 304
notes.evidence: A brush block, which is normally mounted on the engine just behind the propeller, is used to transfer electricity to the slip ring. A slip ring and brush block assembly is shown in Figure 7-29. The slip ring rotates with the propeller and provides a current path to the blade deice boots.

notes.front: Cycling timers energise the heating element circuits for periods of {{c1::15 to 30 seconds}}, with a complete cycle time of 2 minutes.
notes.explanation: Power is applied intermittently, to shed ice after it forms but before it builds up too far.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Deicing Systems”, PDF p. 305
notes.evidence: Cycling timers are used to energize the heating element circuits for periods of 15 to 30 seconds, with a complete cycle time of 2 minutes.

notes.front: When may a propeller deicing system be operated?
notes.back: Only with the propellers rotating, and for short test periods such as the takeoff check or an inspection.
notes.explanation: The restriction is there to prevent the elements overheating.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Deicing Systems”, PDF p. 305
notes.evidence: To prevent element overheating, the propeller deicing system is used only when the propellers are rotating and for short test periods of time during the takeoff check list or system inspection.

notes.front: Per AC 43.13-1B, how should propeller deicing components be repaired?
notes.back: Only as the manufacturer recommends, using replacement parts approved under part 21.
notes.explanation: Repairs outside the manufacturer's recommendations should not be made.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 8-78, p. 8-44
notes.evidence: Components used in propeller deicing systems should be inspected, repaired, assembled, and/or tested in accordance with the manufacturer’s recommendations. Only those repairs which are covered by the manufacturer’s recommendations should be made, and only those replacement parts which are approved under part 21 should be used.

notes.front: In a typical synchrophasing system, where do rpm signals come from, and where does the correction go?
notes.back: From a magnetic pickup on each propeller, to an rpm trimming coil on the slower engine's governor.
notes.explanation: The slow engine's rpm is adjusted to match the other propeller.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Synchronization & Synchrophasing”, PDF p. 305
notes.evidence: Input signals representing propeller rpm are received from magnetic pickup on each propeller. The computed input signals are corrected to a command signal and sent to a rpm trimming coil located on the propeller governor of the slow engine.

notes.front: What makes the autofeather solenoid valve dump oil from the propeller cylinder?
notes.back: Two torque switches sensing low torque from the engine.
notes.explanation: Dumping the oil lets the propeller feather; a test-off-arm switch arms the system.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Autofeathering System”, PDF p. 306
notes.evidence: The system uses a solenoid valve to dump oil pressure from the propeller cylinder (this allows the prop to feather) if two torque switches sense low torque from the engine. This system has a test-off-arm switch that is used to arm the system.

notes.front: Who usually specifies the exact interval for propeller inspections?
notes.back: The propeller manufacturer.
notes.explanation: 'Usually' is the handbook's word; propellers must in any case be inspected regularly.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Inspection & Maintenance”, PDF p. 306
notes.evidence: Propellers must be inspected regularly. The exact time interval for particular propeller inspections is usually specified by the propeller manufacturer.

notes.front: What should happen to a propeller after a ground strike or sudden stoppage?
notes.back: Follow the engine and propeller manufacturers' manuals; it should be disassembled and inspected.
notes.explanation: Internal damage may not be visible from outside.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Inspection & Maintenance”, PDF p. 306
notes.evidence: If a propeller is involved in an accident, and a possibility exists that internal damage may have occurred, or if a propeller has had a ground strike or sudden stoppage, the recommendations of the engine and propeller manufacturer's maintenance manual need to be adhered to. The propeller should be disassembled and inspected.

notes.front: Per AC 43.13-1B, what should be done with a propeller that has struck a foreign object in service?
notes.back: Inspect it promptly for damage per the manufacturer's procedures, and repair it to the manufacturer's instructions if needed.
notes.explanation: The circular applies this to all propellers, whatever they are made of.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 8-91, p. 8-45
notes.evidence: Any propeller that has struck a foreign object during service should be promptly inspected for possible damage in accordance with the propeller manufacturer’s prescribed procedures and, if necessary, repaired according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

notes.front: If a propeller is damaged beyond repair limits and must be replaced, what may be installed?
notes.back: The same make and model, or an alternate listed in the equipment list, aircraft specification, type certificate data sheet or supplemental type certificate.
notes.explanation: Replacement must stay within what the aircraft's approval documents allow.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 8-91, p. 8-45
notes.evidence: If the propeller is damaged beyond the repair limits established by the propeller manufacturer and a replacement is necessary, install the same make/model approved or alternate as specified in the equipment list, applicable FAA aircraft specification, TCDS, or Supplemental Type Certificate (STC).

notes.front: On a new fixed-pitch wooden propeller installation, when should the bolts be checked for torque?
notes.back: After the first flight and after the first 25 hours, then at least every 50 hours.
notes.explanation: No definite interval can be set, because moisture in the wood changes bolt torque.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 8-92b, p. 8-46
notes.evidence: On new, fixed-pitch propeller installations, inspect the bolts for proper torque after the first flight and after the first 25 hours of flying. Thereafter, inspect and check the bolts for proper torque at least every 50 hours.

notes.front: What are two methods for inspecting steel propeller blades?
notes.back: Visual and magnetic particle inspection, among others such as fluorescent penetrant.
notes.explanation: A coat of engine oil or rust-preventive compound makes the visual check easier.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Metal Propeller Inspection”, PDF p. 307
notes.evidence: The inspection of steel blades may be accomplished by either visual, fluorescent penetrant or magnetic particle inspection. The visual inspection is easier if the steel blades are covered with engine oil or rust-preventive compound.

notes.front: What size of transverse crack in an aluminium propeller blade is acceptable?
notes.back: None: a transverse crack or flaw of any size is cause for rejection.
notes.explanation: Aluminium blades must be inspected carefully for cracks and other flaws.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Aluminum Propeller Inspection”, PDF p. 307
notes.evidence: Carefully inspect aluminum propellers and blades for cracks and other flaws. A transverse crack or flaw of any size is cause for rejection.

notes.front: How are composite blades checked for delaminations and debonds?
notes.back: By tapping the blade, or the cuff if fitted, with a metal coin and listening for a change in sound.
notes.explanation: A hollow or dead sound means a debond or delamination is likely.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Composite Propeller Inspection”, PDF p. 307
notes.evidence: Composite blades are inspected for delaminations and debonds by tapping the blade or cuff (if applicable) with a metal coin. If an audible change is apparent, sounding hollow or dead, a debond or delamination is likely.

notes.front: Who must perform major repairs on propellers?
notes.back: A certificated propeller repair station; certificated mechanics may not.
notes.explanation: Mechanics' propeller repairs are often limited to minor ones.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Composite Propeller Inspection”, PDF p. 307
notes.evidence: Repairs to propellers are often limited to minor type repairs. Certificated mechanics are not allowed to perform major repairs on propellers. Major repairs need to be accomplished by a certificated propeller repair station.

notes.front: What must be done with a damaged blade whose model number is on the manufacturer's list of blades that cannot be repaired?
notes.back: Reject it.
notes.explanation: In all cases the propeller manufacturer's recommendations are to be followed.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 8-71, p. 8-37
notes.evidence: Reject damaged blades with model numbers which are on the manufacturer’s list of blades that cannot be repaired. Follow the propeller manufacturer’s recommendations in all cases and make repairs in accordance with the latest techniques and best industry practices.

notes.front: Under part 43 Appendix A, is straightening a steel propeller blade a major repair?
notes.back: Yes: any repair to, or straightening of, steel blades is a propeller major repair.
notes.explanation: It heads the regulation's list of propeller major repairs.
notes.source: 14 CFR part 43 (eCFR, current), Appendix A
notes.evidence: (i) Any repairs to, or straightening of steel blades.

notes.front: When may an aluminium blade with dents, nicks or leading-edge pitting be repaired?
notes.back: When the removal or treatment does not materially affect its strength, weight or performance.
notes.explanation: The damage is removed or treated unless the manufacturer says otherwise.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 8-73, p. 8-37
notes.evidence: Aluminum-alloy propellers and blades with dents, cuts, scars, scratches, nicks, leading-edge pitting, etc., may be repaired, provided the removal or treatment does not materially affect the strength, weight, or performance of the blade.

notes.front: What does this repair-limits chart from AC 43.13-1B give a mechanic repairing an aluminium blade?
notes.back: The maximum allowable reduction in blade width and thickness below the minimum dimensions of the blade drawing.
notes.explanation: It is read against the blade's minimum drawing dimensions, not its current size.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 8-73a, p. 8-37
notes.evidence: When repairing blades, Figures 8-26 and 8-27 show the maximum reduction in width and thickness that is allowable below the minimum dimensions required by the blade drawing and blade manufacturing specification.

image.alt: AC 43.13-1B Figure 8-27 chart: horizontal axis is radius as percent of repaired blade radius, 10 to 90; vertical axis is reduction in width and thickness as percent of blade section, 1 to 13. The curve rises from about 2 percent near the root, gently at first, then steeply beyond about 70 percent radius to about 12 percent at 90 percent. A note says the reductions shown are the maximum allowable below the minimum dimensions required by the blade drawing and blade manufacturing specification.

notes.front: When repairs reduce an aluminium blade's width or thickness below the repair limits, what must be done?
notes.back: Reject the blade.
notes.explanation: The limits come from the blade manufacturing specification.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 8-74, p. 8-41
notes.evidence: When repairs reduce the width or thickness of the blade below these limits, reject the blade.

notes.front: Is shortening propeller blades a major or a minor repair?
notes.back: A major repair.
notes.explanation: The size of the job does not matter: shortening is classed as major.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 8-73b, p. 8-40
notes.evidence: Shortening propeller blades is a major repair.

notes.front: What limits how far a propeller's diameter may be reduced by shortening?
notes.back: The minimum diameter in the pertinent specification or type certificate data sheet.
notes.explanation: Going below that figure is not permissible in any repair.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 8-73b, p. 8-40
notes.evidence: In making the repair, it is not permissible to reduce the propeller diameter below the minimum diameter limit shown on the pertinent specification or Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS).

notes.front: Why must a blade that shows discoloration from heating be rejected?
notes.back: Only cold straightening is authorised, so blades heated for any repair must be rejected.
notes.explanation: Discoloration is the sign of unauthorised heating to look for.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 8-93c(3), p. 8-47
notes.evidence: Blades should be examined for any discoloration that would indicate unauthorized heating. Blades that have been heated for any repair must be rejected since only cold straightening is authorized.

notes.front: How does vibration caused by a propeller's balance, angle or track typically behave across the rpm range?
notes.back: It typically occurs throughout the whole rpm range, though its intensity may vary.
notes.explanation: Many other sources of vibration exist, which can make troubleshooting difficult.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Vibration”, PDF p. 308
notes.evidence: If a propeller vibrates, whether due to balance, angle, or track problems, it typically vibrates throughout the entire rpm range, although the intensity of the vibration may vary with the rpm.

notes.front: Is blade shake a source of vibration problems?
notes.back: No; once the engine runs, centrifugal force holds the blades firmly against their bearings.
notes.explanation: The holding force is roughly 30,000 to 40,000 pounds.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Vibration”, PDF p. 308
notes.evidence: Blade shake is not the source of vibration problems. Once the engine is running, centrifugal force holds the blades firmly (approximately 30,000–40,000 pounds) against blade bearings.

notes.front: In what order is a vibrating propeller checked, and what if both checks pass?
notes.back: Tracking first, then the low-pitch blade angle; if both are correct, it is statically or dynamically unbalanced.
notes.explanation: An unbalanced propeller is then replaced, or rebalanced if the manufacturer allows.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Vibration”, PDF p. 308
notes.evidence: Check the propeller blade tracking and then the low-pitch blade angle setting to determine if either is the cause of the vibration. If both propeller tracking and low blade angle setting are correct, the propeller is statically or dynamically unbalanced and should be replaced, or rebalanced if permitted by the manufacturer.

notes.front: In the simple tracking check, each blade track should be within {{c1::1/16 inch}} (plus or minus) of the opposite blade's track.
notes.explanation: The manufacturer's own tolerance must not be exceeded in any case.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 8-108e, p. 8-51
notes.evidence: Each blade track should be within 1/16-inch (plus or minus) from the opposite blade’s track.

notes.front: What are two things that can put a propeller out of track?
notes.back: A bent blade and a bent propeller flange, among others such as wrongly torqued mounting bolts.
notes.explanation: Bolts may be either over- or under-torqued.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Blade Tracking”, PDF p. 309
notes.evidence: An out-of-track propeller, may be due to one or more propeller blades being bent, a bent propeller flange, or propeller mounting bolts that are either over- or undertorqued.

notes.front: Why must metal scribes never be used to mark blade stations on a propeller?
notes.back: Surface scratches act as stress concentrators that can eventually lead to blade failure.
notes.explanation: Any sharply pointed instrument carries the same risk.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Checking & Adjusting Propeller Blade Angles”, PDF p. 309
notes.evidence: Do not use metal scribes or other sharply pointed instruments to mark the location of blade stations or make reference lines on propeller blades, since such surface scratches can induce failure (stress concentrator), eventually resulting in blade failure.

notes.front: On the universal propeller protractor, what do the vernier graduations represent?
notes.back: Tenths of a degree; ten vernier points equal nine points on the degree scale.
notes.explanation: The degree scale itself shows whole degrees.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Universal Propeller Protractor”, PDF p. 310
notes.evidence: In determining the blade angle, remember that ten points on the vernier scale are equal to nine points on the degree scale. The graduations on the vernier scale represent tenths of a degree, but those of the degree scale represent whole degrees.

notes.front: In what positions is a two-bladed propeller checked for static balance?
notes.back: Blades vertical, then horizontal, then vertical again with the blades swapped end for end.
notes.explanation: The repeat vertical check puts the blade that was down in the up position.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Static Balancing”, PDF p. 310
notes.evidence: Check two-bladed propeller assemblies for balance: first with the blades in a vertical position and then with the blades in a horizontal position. Repeat the vertical position check with the blade positions reversed; that is, with the blade that was checked in the downward position placed in the upward position.

notes.front: What can dynamic balancing correct, and what can it not?
notes.back: Only mass unbalance of the external rotating parts; it cannot fix an engine or aircraft in poor mechanical condition.
notes.explanation: Defective, worn or loose parts make balancing impossible.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Dynamic Balancing”, PDF p. 311
notes.evidence: Dynamic balancing only improves the vibration caused by mass unbalance of the externally rotating components of the propulsion system. Balancing does not reduce the vibration level if the engine or aircraft is in poor mechanical condition. Defective, worn, or loose parts will make balancing impossible.

notes.front: What are the three major types of propeller shaft?
notes.back: Tapered, splined and flanged.
notes.explanation: Tapered shafts are identified by taper numbers, while splined and flanged shafts are identified by SAE numbers.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 1, “Propeller Reduction Gearing & Propeller Shafts”, PDF p. 44
notes.evidence: may be of three major types: tapered, splined, or flanged. Tapered shafts are identified by taper numbers.

notes.front: What must not be used to clean aluminium and steel propeller blades?
notes.back: Acid or caustic materials, or tools such as steel wool that scratch or mar the blade.
notes.explanation: Power buffers and steel brushes are also to be avoided.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Cleaning Propeller Blades”, PDF p. 313
notes.evidence: Do not use acid or caustic materials. Power buffers, steel wool, steel brushes, or any other tool or substance that may scratch or mar the blade should be avoided.

notes.front: What is the preferred medium for charging a propeller air dome?
notes.back: Nitrogen.
notes.explanation: Dry air is the alternative the handbook allows.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Charging the Propeller Air Dome”, PDF p. 313
notes.evidence: then charge the cylinder with dry air or nitrogen. The air charge valve is located on the cylinder as indicated in Figure 7-41. Nitrogen is the preferred charging medium.

notes.front: Why must the manufacturer's propeller greasing schedule be followed?
notes.back: Water sometimes gets into blade bearings, so greasing both lubricates and protects against corrosion.
notes.explanation: Experience with some models is what showed water getting in.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Lubrication”, PDF p. 313
notes.evidence: Experience indicates that water sometimes gets into the propeller blade bearing assembly on some models of propellers. For this reason, the propeller manufacturer’s greasing schedule must be followed to ensure proper lubrication of moving parts and protection from corrosion.

notes.front: In the handbook's example, at what interval must the propeller be lubricated?
notes.back: Not more than 100 hours or 12 calendar months, whichever occurs first.
notes.explanation: Lubrication intervals matter because of corrosion.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Lubrication”, PDF p. 314
notes.evidence: The propeller must be lubricated at intervals not to exceed 100 hours or at 12 calendar months, whichever occurs first.

notes.front: Why must static balance weights placed on the hub at overhaul not be moved during later dynamic balancing?
notes.back: They are part of the basic hub assembly.
notes.explanation: They go on the hub areas of each light blade socket.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Prop Reassembly”, PDF p. 315
notes.evidence: These weights should be considered part of the basic hub assembly and should not be moved during subsequent dynamic balancing to the engine.

notes.front: If a propeller is hunting, what are two items an appropriately licensed repair facility should check?
notes.back: The governor and the fuel control, among others such as the synchrophaser.
notes.explanation: All three are sources the handbook lists for hunting.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Hunting & Surging”, PDF p. 316
notes.evidence: If propeller is hunting, an appropriately licensed repair facility should check: 1. Governor, 2. Fuel control, and 3. Synchrophaser or synchronizer.

notes.front: A propeller fails to feather or feathers slowly. What are two things the technician checks?
notes.back: The air charge, if lost or low, and the function and rigging of the propeller-governor control linkage.
notes.explanation: The governor drain function is checked as well.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Failure to Feather or Feathers Slowly”, PDF p. 316
notes.evidence: Refer to the air charge section in the maintenance manual if the air charge is lost or low. 2. Check for proper function and rigging of propeller/ governor control linkage. 3. Check the governor drain function.

notes.front: What happens when a turboprop's power lever is moved below the start position?
notes.back: The propeller pitch reverses to give reverse thrust for rapid deceleration after landing.
notes.explanation: This happens within the beta range of the quadrant.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Turboprop Engines & Propeller Control Systems”, PDF p. 317
notes.evidence: When the power lever is moved below the start position, the propeller pitch is reversed to provide reverse thrust for rapid deceleration of the aircraft after landing.

notes.front: On a turboprop in flight, to what are power changes related, rather than to engine speed?
notes.back: To turbine inlet temperature.
notes.explanation: In flight the propeller holds engine speed constant, so speed cannot be the measure of power.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Turboprop Engines & Propeller Control Systems”, PDF p. 317
notes.evidence: A characteristic of the turboprop is that changes in power are not related to engine speed, but to turbine inlet temperature. During flight, the propeller maintains a constant engine speed.

notes.front: What two jobs does a turboprop propeller brake do?
notes.back: It stops a feathered propeller windmilling in flight and shortens the time to stop after shutdown.
notes.explanation: It is often built into the reduction gearbox.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Reduction Gear Assembly”, PDF p. 317
notes.evidence: A propeller brake is often incorporated into the gearbox. The propeller brake is designed to prevent the propeller from windmilling when it is feathered in flight, and to decrease the time for the propeller to come to a complete stop after engine shutdown.

notes.front: In this Hartzell turboprop system, what does rising oil pressure do, and what acts when it falls?
notes.back: Rising pressure drives the blades to low pitch; when it falls, the return spring and flyweights push them to high pitch.
notes.explanation: Oil moves the servo piston forward, compressing the feather spring.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Pratt & Whitney PT6 Hartzell Propeller System”, PDF p. 318
notes.evidence: When oil pressure is decreased, the return spring and flyweights force the oil out of the servo piston and change the blade pitch to a high pitch position. An increase in oil pressure drives the blades towards low pitch.

notes.front: What does the lock-pitch solenoid valve prevent?
notes.back: The propeller going into reverse or below the primary blade angle if the beta system fails in flight.
notes.explanation: It cycles as a backup to the beta valve.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Pratt & Whitney PT6 Hartzell Propeller System”, PDF p. 319
notes.evidence: The lock-pitch solenoid valve prevents the propeller from going into reverse or below the primary blade angle in the event of a beta system malfunction in flight.

notes.front: In reverse on this system, how is propeller speed controlled?
notes.back: By limiting engine power, with propeller speed held 5 percent below the selected speed.
notes.explanation: Blade angle is no longer used to control speed in this mode.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Pratt & Whitney PT6 Hartzell Propeller System”, PDF p. 319
notes.evidence: In reverse, propeller speed remains 5 percent below the selected propeller speed so that the control valve remains fully open, and only the beta valve controls the oil flow to the propeller dome. In this mode, the propeller speed is no longer controlled by changing the blade angle. It is now controlled by limiting engine power.

notes.front: The Hydromatic propeller has no flyweights. What turns its blades to a lower angle?
notes.back: Oil pressure together with the blades' centrifugal twisting moment.
notes.explanation: Its moving parts are completely enclosed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Pratt & Whitney PT6 Hartzell Propeller System”, PDF p. 320
notes.evidence: In the hydromatic propeller, no flyweights are used, and the moving parts of the mechanism are completely enclosed. Oil pressure and the centrifugal twisting moment of the blades are used together to turn the blades to a lower angle.

notes.front: How is a Hydromatic propeller unfeathered, and when is the pump shut off?
notes.back: Hold the feathering push-button in; the operator shuts off the pump at about 1,000 engine rpm.
notes.explanation: As the blades unfeather they windmill, which helps the process.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Unfeathering Operation”, PDF p. 325
notes.evidence: When the engine speed has increased to approximately 1,000 rpm, the operator shuts off the feathering pump motor.

notes.front: What does the adjustable stop on a propeller governor limit?
notes.back: The maximum speed at which the engine can run.
notes.explanation: Once takeoff rpm is reached the propeller moves off its low-pitch stop.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Setting the Propeller Governor”, PDF p. 326
notes.evidence: The propeller governor incorporates an adjustable stop that limits the maximum speed at which the engine can run. As soon as the takeoff rpm is reached, the propeller moves off the low-pitch stop.
