notes.front: When turning a propeller by hand, where must you not stand?
notes.back: Within the arc of the propeller blades.
notes.explanation: The engine could fire while the propeller is being turned.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 8, “Depreservation of an Engine”, PDF p. 347
notes.evidence: Do not stand within the arc of the propeller blades while turning the propeller.

notes.front: With power unchanged, a propeller's blade angle is reduced. What happens to its speed?
notes.back: B) It speeds up
notes.choices:
A) It slows down
B) It speeds up
C) It stays the same because power is unchanged
D) It stops
notes.choicesExplained: A) Slowing down follows an increase in blade angle, not a decrease. C) Blade angle changes the load, so speed does change. D) Nothing about a smaller angle stops the propeller.
notes.explanation: A smaller angle means less load on the engine, so the same power turns it faster.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Aerodynamic Factors”, PDF p. 290
notes.evidence: If the blade angle is decreased, the propeller speeds up. Thus, the engine rpm can be controlled by increasing or decreasing the blade angle.

notes.front: An owner says a small nick on the blade face is 'only cosmetic'. Why does the handbook treat nicks and scratches as potentially serious?
notes.back: C) They could lead to cracks and failure of the blade
notes.choices:
A) They increase the propeller's slip
B) They change the geometric pitch
C) They could lead to cracks and failure of the blade
D) They reduce the governing range
notes.choicesExplained: A) Slip depends on how the propeller moves through air, not on nicks. B) Geometric pitch comes from blade angle and radius. D) The governing range is set by the speeder spring.
notes.explanation: The blade face is under tension from centrifugal force and bending, so a nick is a starting point for a crack.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Basic Propeller Principles”, PDF p. 290
notes.evidence: For these reasons, nicks or scratches on the blade may cause very serious consequences. These could lead to cracks and failure of the blade

notes.front: On the Hartzell nonfeathering aluminium-hub model whose governor oil drives the blades to high pitch, governor oil pressure is lost. Which way do the blades tend to go?
notes.back: D) Towards low pitch (high rpm)
notes.choices:
A) Into feather
B) Towards high pitch
C) They lock where they are
D) Towards low pitch (high rpm)
notes.choicesExplained: A) This model is nonfeathering. B) High pitch needs the governor oil that has been lost. C) Nothing locks the blades; a twisting moment still acts on them.
notes.explanation: Without oil, only the centrifugal twisting moment is left acting, and it pulls towards low pitch.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Hartzell Constant-Speed, Nonfeathering”, PDF p. 300
notes.evidence: The centrifugal twisting moment of the blades tends to move them into low pitch (high rpm) in the absence of governor oil pressure.

notes.front: Which of these forces tends to turn a rotating propeller's blades towards a high blade angle?
notes.back: D) Aerodynamic twisting force
notes.choices:
A) Centrifugal twisting force
B) Torque bending force
C) Thrust bending force
D) Aerodynamic twisting force
notes.choicesExplained: A) Centrifugal twisting turns blades towards low angle. B) Torque bending bends blades against rotation. C) Thrust bending bends blades forward.
notes.explanation: Only one of the four twists the blade, and in the high-angle direction.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Basic Propeller Principles”, PDF p. 289
notes.evidence: Aerodynamic twisting force tends to turn the blades to a high blade angle.

notes.front: A propeller would advance 80 inches per revolution with no slippage but actually advances 68 inches. What is its slip?
notes.back: C) 12 inches
notes.choices:
A) 148 inches
B) 80 inches
C) 12 inches
D) 68 inches
notes.choicesExplained: A) Adding the two figures has no meaning. B) 80 inches is the geometric pitch. D) 68 inches is the effective pitch.
notes.explanation: Slip is geometric pitch minus effective pitch: 80 − 68 = 12 inches.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Aerodynamic Process”, PDF p. 288
notes.evidence: Geometric pitch - Effective pitch = slip

notes.front: A manufacturer specifies checking blade angle at the 36-inch station. Where is that?
notes.back: B) 36 inches from the propeller's centre of hub
notes.choices:
A) 36 inches in from the blade tip
B) 36 inches from the propeller's centre of hub
C) 36 percent of the propeller diameter
D) 36 inches from the engine flange face
notes.choicesExplained: A) Stations are counted from the hub, not the tip. C) A station is a distance in inches, not a percentage. D) The reference is the hub centre, not the flange face.
notes.explanation: Station numbers are inches measured out from the centre of the hub.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Basic Propeller Principles”, PDF p. 289
notes.evidence: For purposes of analysis, a blade can be divided into segments that are located by station numbers in inches from the center of the blade hub.

notes.front: An aircraft with a constant-speed propeller is pushed into a dive at an unchanged throttle. What should the blade angle do?
notes.back: A) Increase enough to prevent overspeeding
notes.choices:
A) Increase enough to prevent overspeeding
B) Go to feather
C) Decrease, to raise rpm
D) Stay fixed, letting rpm rise
notes.choicesExplained: C) Decreasing the angle is the climb response and would make an overspeed worse. B) Feathering is for an engine failure, not a dive. D) Holding the angle would let the engine overspeed, which the governor prevents.
notes.explanation: Power output stays the same because rpm is held constant by the larger angle.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Constant-Speed Propellers”, PDF p. 293
notes.evidence: When the aircraft goes into a dive, the blade angle increases sufficiently to prevent overspeeding and, with the same throttle setting, the power output remains unchanged.

notes.front: An aircraft with a constant-speed propeller pitches nose-up at a fixed throttle, and rpm starts to fall below the selected value. What do the governor flyweights and pilot valve do?
notes.back: B) Flyweights tilt inward; pilot valve moves down to send oil for lower pitch
notes.choices:
A) Flyweights tilt outward; pilot valve rises to drain oil
B) Flyweights tilt inward; pilot valve moves down to send oil for lower pitch
C) Flyweights stay balanced; no oil moves
D) Flyweights tilt inward; pilot valve rises to feather the blades
notes.choicesExplained: A) Outward flyweights and a rising valve are the overspeed response. C) A balanced state is on-speed, which a falling rpm is not. D) Inward flyweights let the spring push the valve down, not up, and feathering is not the aim.
notes.explanation: This is an underspeed: the speeder spring wins, and lower pitch lets rpm recover.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Underspeed Condition”, PDF p. 295
notes.evidence: In this condition, the flyweights tilt inward because there is not enough centrifugal force on the flyweights to overcome the force of the speeder spring. The pilot valve, forced down by the speeder spring, meters oil flow to decrease propeller pitch and raise engine rpm.

notes.front: A pilot eases the propeller control aft to a lower rpm at an unchanged throttle. Before the blades move, which governor condition exists?
notes.back: C) Overspeed
notes.choices:
A) On-speed
B) Underspeed
C) Overspeed
D) Feathered
notes.choicesExplained: B) Underspeed means the engine is below the set rpm, but it is now above it. A) On-speed needs the forces balanced, which the new setting has upset. D) Nothing here feathers the propeller.
notes.explanation: The engine is now running above the newly set rpm, which is what overspeed means.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Overspeed Condition”, PDF p. 297
notes.evidence: When the engine is operating above the rpm set by the pilot using the flight deck control, the governor is operating in an overspeed condition.

notes.front: A governor's flyweight force exactly balances the speeder spring, and the pilot valve sends no oil either way. Which condition is this?
notes.back: C) On-speed
notes.choices:
A) Underspeed
B) Overspeed
C) On-speed
D) Feathering
notes.choicesExplained: A) Underspeed has the spring winning and oil going to lower pitch. B) Overspeed has the flyweights winning and oil draining. D) Feathering is a propeller position, not a governor balance state.
notes.explanation: Balanced forces and a centred pilot valve define on-speed; the blades are not changing pitch.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “On-Speed Condition”, PDF p. 297
notes.evidence: In the on-speed condition, the forces of the governor flyweights and the tension on the speeder spring are equal; the propeller blades are not moving or changing pitch.

notes.front: An engine on a twin fails in cruise. Why would the crew feather its propeller?
notes.back: A) To turn the blades parallel to the line of flight and greatly reduce drag
notes.choices:
A) To turn the blades parallel to the line of flight and greatly reduce drag
B) To give reverse thrust
C) To keep the governor on-speed
D) To keep the dead engine turning for a quick restart
notes.choicesExplained: D) Feathering stops the propeller turning, with minimum windmilling. B) Reverse is a negative blade angle used on the ground. C) The governor's state is not the reason for feathering.
notes.explanation: Edge-on blades stop the propeller turning and cut drag from the dead engine.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Feathering Propellers”, PDF p. 294
notes.evidence: By rotating the propeller blade angle parallel to the line of flight, the drag on the aircraft is greatly reduced. With the blades parallel to the airstream, the propeller stops turning and minimum windmilling, if any, occurs.

notes.front: On a twin with constant-speed feathering propellers, an engine loses all oil pressure through a broken part and the pilot has not yet noticed. What does that propeller do?
notes.back: D) It feathers automatically
notes.choices:
A) It goes into reverse
B) It goes to full low pitch
C) It stays at the last blade angle
D) It feathers automatically
notes.choicesExplained: B) Low pitch needs governor oil, which is gone. C) The internal forces drain the oil and move the blades. A) Reverse needs deliberate power-lever action on types that have it.
notes.explanation: The governor's oil comes from the engine, so lost engine oil pressure means the propeller feathers.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Constant-Speed Feathering Propeller”, PDF p. 302
notes.evidence: As the governor obtains its supply of oil from the engine lubricating system, it follows that if the engine runs out of oil or if oil pressure fails due to breakage of a part of the engine, the propeller feathers automatically.

notes.front: A flight school's twin must unfeather quickly in flight for engine-failure training, without waiting for a cranking engine to build governor oil pressure. Which system fits best?
notes.back: D) An unfeathering accumulator
notes.choices:
A) A test club
B) A synchrophaser
C) A slinger ring
D) An unfeathering accumulator
notes.choicesExplained: A) A test club is for breaking in engines on a stand. C) A slinger ring carries anti-icing fluid. B) A synchrophaser matches blade phase between engines.
notes.explanation: The accumulator's stored charge unfeathers in a very short time and starts the engine windmilling.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Unfeathering”, PDF p. 302
notes.evidence: This system is used with training aircraft because it unfeathers the propeller in a very short time and starts the engine windmilling.

notes.front: A turboprop crew want to spare their wheel brakes on landing. With the gear on the runway, what propeller action helps?
notes.back: B) Move the blades to negative pitch and apply power
notes.choices:
A) Feather both propellers
B) Move the blades to negative pitch and apply power
C) Select the highest forward pitch
D) Switch on the synchrophaser
notes.choicesExplained: A) Feathered blades give almost no braking force. C) High forward pitch still gives forward thrust. D) Synchrophasing only matches blade phase.
notes.explanation: Reverse thrust brakes the aircraft aerodynamically and reduces brake wear.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Reverse-Pitch Propellers”, PDF p. 294
notes.evidence: Normally, when the landing gear is in contact with the runway after landing, the propellers blades can be moved to negative pitch (reversed), which creates thrust opposite of the aircraft direction and slows the aircraft. As the propeller blades move into negative pitch, engine power is applied to increase the negative thrust.

notes.front: After a normal shutdown, a mechanic measures a fixed-turbine turboprop's blades at about 1.5°. In the handbook's typical range, which position are they in?
notes.back: D) On the locks
notes.choices:
A) Feather
B) Flight idle
C) Reverse
D) On the locks
notes.choicesExplained: A) Feather is 85 to 90°. B) Flight idle is 10 to 12°. C) Reverse is negative, −2 to −8°.
notes.explanation: Fixed turboprops are shut down on the locks, typically 1 to 2°.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Figure 7-3, Propeller range positions”, PDF p. 288
notes.evidence: Fixed turboprop engines are shut down on the locks to prevent load on the engine during restart.

notes.front: An amphibian has its engine on a pylon above the wing, with the propeller on the rear end of the drive shaft behind the engine. What kind of propeller is it?
notes.back: A) Pusher
notes.choices:
A) Pusher
B) Tractor
C) Test club
D) Ground-adjustable
notes.choicesExplained: B) A tractor sits on the upstream end, in front of the structure. C) A test club is a break-in propeller for test stands. D) Ground-adjustable describes pitch setting, not location.
notes.explanation: Mounting on the downstream end behind the structure is what defines a pusher.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Pusher Propellers”, PDF p. 292
notes.evidence: Pusher propellers are those mounted on the downstream end of a drive shaft behind the supporting structure.

notes.front: A propeller's blade angle can be changed in flight, but only when the pilot moves it, and it then stays until the pilot changes it again. What type is it?
notes.back: D) Controllable-pitch
notes.choices:
A) Ground-adjustable
B) Constant-speed
C) Fixed-pitch
D) Controllable-pitch
notes.choicesExplained: B) A constant-speed propeller changes angle by itself through a governor. C) A fixed-pitch propeller cannot change angle at all. A) A ground-adjustable propeller can be reset only when not turning.
notes.explanation: Direct pilot control with no governor marks the controllable-pitch type.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Controllable-Pitch Propeller”, PDF p. 293
notes.evidence: With the controllable-pitch type, the blade angle can be changed in flight, but the pilot must change the propeller blade angle directly. The blade angle will not change again until the pilot changes it.

notes.front: An owner wants the cheapest, simplest propeller needing no pilot input in flight for a low-powered single-engine aircraft. Which type fits?
notes.back: C) Fixed-pitch
notes.choices:
A) Constant-speed
B) Reverse-pitch
C) Fixed-pitch
D) Controllable-pitch
notes.choicesExplained: A) A constant-speed propeller needs a governor and pilot rpm selection. B) Reversing is a refinement mainly for turboprops. D) Controllable pitch needs the pilot to change the angle.
notes.explanation: Low expense and simple operation are the fixed-pitch propeller's advantages.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Fixed-Pitch Propeller”, PDF p. 292
notes.evidence: Many singleengine aircraft use fixed-pitch propellers and the advantages of these are less expense and their simple operation. This type of propeller does not require any control inputs from the pilot in flight.

notes.front: A wooden propeller has water trapped under its metal tipping, and the small holes near the tip are clogged with paint. What should be done?
notes.back: B) Open the holes; they must be kept open at all times
notes.choices:
A) Seal the holes to keep water out
B) Open the holes; they must be kept open at all times
C) Replace the tipping with fabric
D) Nothing; the water will evaporate in flight
notes.choicesExplained: A) Sealing would trap the moisture the holes let out. C) Fabric does not replace the tipping's protective job. D) The holes are what let moisture escape, so leaving them blocked is wrong.
notes.explanation: The holes let condensed moisture drain away or be thrown out by centrifugal force.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Fixed-Pitch Wooden Propellers”, PDF p. 299
notes.evidence: Since moisture condenses on the tipping between the metal and the wood, the tipping is provided with small holes near the blade tip to allow this moisture to drain away or be thrown out by centrifugal force. It is important that these drain holes be kept open at all times.

notes.front: An owner asks a mechanic to change the pitch of a one-piece metal fixed-pitch propeller slightly. Who does the handbook say can do it?
notes.back: A) A propeller repair station, within limits, by twisting the blade
notes.choices:
A) A propeller repair station, within limits, by twisting the blade
B) The mechanic on the aircraft, by bending the tip
C) Any pilot, with a protractor
D) Nobody; metal fixed-pitch pitch can never change
notes.choicesExplained: C) The handbook gives this job to a propeller repair station, not a pilot. B) Bending the tip is not the method described. D) The handbook says pitch can be changed, within limits.
notes.explanation: Having no joint between blades and hub is why the blade itself can be twisted.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Metal Fixed-Pitch Propellers”, PDF p. 299
notes.evidence: because there was no joint between the blades and the hub, the propeller pitch could be changed, within limits, by twisting the blade slightly by a propeller repair station.

notes.front: A feathering propeller feathers slowly. Air charge, linkage rigging and governor drain are all fine. What remains, and who deals with it?
notes.back: D) Misadjustment or internal corrosion causing friction, at a licensed propeller repair facility
notes.choices:
A) A tachometer error, fixed by the mechanic
B) A spinner wobble, fixed by shimming
C) Low deice current, fixed at the timer
D) Misadjustment or internal corrosion causing friction, at a licensed propeller repair facility
notes.choicesExplained: A) Tachometer error does not slow feathering. B) Spinner wobble is a balance issue, not a feathering one. C) Deice current has nothing to do with feathering speed.
notes.explanation: Excess friction inside the propeller must be checked at an appropriately licensed facility.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Failure to Feather or Feathers Slowly”, PDF p. 316
notes.evidence: Check the propeller for misadjustment or internal corrosion (usually in blade bearings or pitch change mechanism) that results in excessive friction. This must be performed at an appropriately licensed propeller repair facility.

notes.front: To trace a fault, a mechanic plans to leave the propeller deice system switched on for ten minutes with the engines stopped. What is wrong?
notes.back: C) The elements may overheat; it is for rotating propellers or short tests only
notes.choices:
A) Nothing; long runs are normal on the ground
B) The slinger ring will overflow
C) The elements may overheat; it is for rotating propellers or short tests only
D) It will feather the propellers
notes.choicesExplained: A) Long ground runs with stopped propellers are exactly what the handbook rules out. B) The slinger ring belongs to fluid anti-icing, not electric deicing. D) Deicing has no link to feathering.
notes.explanation: Use is limited to rotating propellers and short test periods to prevent element overheating.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Deicing Systems”, PDF p. 305
notes.evidence: To prevent element overheating, the propeller deicing system is used only when the propellers are rotating and for short test periods of time during the takeoff check list or system inspection.

notes.front: On a fluid anti-icing system, a blade's feed shoe is missing. Where will the fluid tend to go?
notes.back: D) Towards areas where ice does not collect in large quantities
notes.choices:
A) Nowhere; flow stops
B) Straight along the leading edge to the tip
C) Back into the slinger ring
D) Towards areas where ice does not collect in large quantities
notes.choicesExplained: B) Guiding fluid along the leading edge is what the missing shoe did. C) Centrifugal force carries fluid outward, not back to the ring. A) Fluid still reaches the shank through the nozzles.
notes.explanation: Airflow round the shank disperses the fluid; the shoe channels it where ice forms.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Anti-Icing Systems”, PDF p. 303
notes.evidence: Because airflow around a blade shank tends to disperse anti-icing fluids to areas where ice does not collect in large quantities, feed shoes, or boots, are installed on the blade leading edge.

notes.front: A twin's propellers turn at the same rpm, yet passengers still notice noise from the blades' relative positions. Which system addresses this?
notes.back: C) Synchrophasing
notes.choices:
A) Autofeather
B) Beta range
C) Synchrophasing
D) A test club
notes.choicesExplained: A) Autofeather feathers a failed engine's propeller. B) Beta is a turboprop ground range. D) A test club breaks in engines.
notes.explanation: Synchrophasing sets a blade phase relationship between left and right propellers to reduce cabin noise.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Synchronization & Synchrophasing”, PDF p. 305
notes.evidence: It functions to match the rpm of both engines and establish a blade phase relationship between the left and right propellers to reduce cabin noise.

notes.front: In cruise with the power lever well back, an engine fails on a twin with autofeather armed. Why may the propeller not autofeather?
notes.back: C) It works only with the power lever near or in the takeoff position
notes.choices:
A) The torque switches only work on the ground
B) Autofeather needs the beta range
C) It works only with the power lever near or in the takeoff position
D) Autofeather only acts on reverse-pitch propellers
notes.choicesExplained: A) The system works in flight during takeoff, approach and landing, so its torque switches are not ground-only. B) Beta is a ground-handling range. D) The handbook limits it by power lever position, not propeller type.
notes.explanation: The system is switch-armed for takeoff and needs the power lever near or at takeoff.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Autofeathering System”, PDF p. 306
notes.evidence: This system is switch-armed for use during takeoff and can function only when the power lever is near or in the “takeoff” position.

notes.front: A taxiing aircraft's propeller strikes a runway light. What should the mechanic do?
notes.back: D) Follow the manufacturers' manuals; the propeller should be disassembled and inspected
notes.choices:
A) Straighten any bent blade and return it to service
B) Dress the tips and fly it
C) Only a daily visual check is needed
D) Follow the manufacturers' manuals; the propeller should be disassembled and inspected
notes.choicesExplained: A) Straightening a damaged propeller is never done in the field. B) Dressing the tips ignores possible internal damage. C) A strike needs more than a routine check.
notes.explanation: A ground strike may cause internal damage that a visual check cannot show.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Inspection & Maintenance”, PDF p. 306
notes.evidence: if a propeller has had a ground strike or sudden stoppage, the recommendations of the engine and propeller manufacturer's maintenance manual need to be adhered to. The propeller should be disassembled and inspected.

notes.front: A propeller damaged beyond limits must be replaced, and the owner wants a different model. Where does the mechanic confirm the alternate is approved?
notes.back: A) The equipment list, aircraft specification, type certificate data sheet or supplemental type certificate
notes.choices:
A) The equipment list, aircraft specification, type certificate data sheet or supplemental type certificate
B) The propeller logbook
C) Any service bulletin for a similar aircraft
D) The pilot's operating preferences
notes.choicesExplained: B) The logbook records work done; it does not approve models. C) A bulletin for another aircraft does not approve an installation. D) Preference has no approval status.
notes.explanation: Only models approved in the aircraft's approval documents may be installed.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 8-91, p. 8-45
notes.evidence: install the same make/model approved or alternate as specified in the equipment list, applicable FAA aircraft specification, TCDS, or Supplemental Type Certificate (STC).

notes.front: To dress out tip damage, a shop proposes shortening a set of blades so the diameter falls just below the minimum in the type certificate data sheet. Is this acceptable?
notes.back: A) No; diameter may not go below the minimum in the specification or data sheet
notes.choices:
A) No; diameter may not go below the minimum in the specification or data sheet
B) Yes, if all blades are shortened equally
C) Yes, if the tips are rounded
D) Yes, if the mechanic signs it off
notes.choicesExplained: B) Shortening every blade is required, but the minimum diameter still applies. C) Tip shape does not change the diameter limit. D) No signature makes a below-minimum diameter permissible.
notes.explanation: The specification or data sheet sets a floor on diameter for any shortening repair.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 8-73b, p. 8-40
notes.evidence: In making the repair, it is not permissible to reduce the propeller diameter below the minimum diameter limit shown on the pertinent specification or Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS).

notes.front: Inspecting a wooden propeller, a mechanic sees a fine line in the fabric covering near the tip. What may it indicate?
notes.back: C) A crack in the wood
notes.choices:
A) Normal fabric texture
B) A loose lag screw
C) A crack in the wood
D) Excess varnish
notes.choicesExplained: A) The handbook treats a fine line as a warning, not normal texture. B) Lag screws are at the metal sleeve, not under the tip fabric. D) Excess varnish is not what the handbook links to fine lines.
notes.explanation: Cracks usually start at the leading edge, and a fine line in the covering may show one.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Wood Propeller Inspection”, PDF p. 307
notes.evidence: A fine line appearing in the fabric or plastic may indicate a crack in the wood.

notes.front: A wooden propeller aircraft has been stored in a damp hangar and then flown in hot, dry weather. What should the mechanic check first at the hub?
notes.back: D) Hub bolt torque
notes.choices:
A) Blade track only
B) Governor setting
C) Tip fabric colour
D) Hub bolt torque
notes.choicesExplained: A) Tracking will not show hub shrinkage. C) Fabric colour has nothing to do with bolt tightness. B) A fixed-pitch wooden propeller has no governor.
notes.explanation: Swelling then drying crushes fibres and shrinks the hub, loosening the bolts.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 8-92b, p. 8-46
notes.evidence: Later, when the propeller dries out during dry weather or due to heat from the engine, a certain amount of propeller hub shrinkage takes place, and the wood no longer completely fills the space between the two hub flanges. Consequently, the hub bolts become loose.

notes.front: During a 100-hour inspection, a mechanic finds a fine crack running across an aluminium blade, about 1/8 inch long. What is the outcome?
notes.back: B) Reject the blade
notes.choices:
A) Dress it out with a file
B) Reject the blade
C) Monitor it at the next inspection
D) Stop-drill it
notes.choicesExplained: A) Dressing is for nicks and scratches within limits, not transverse cracks. D) Stop-drilling is not a propeller blade repair here. C) Any size of transverse crack means rejection now.
notes.explanation: A transverse crack of any size is cause for rejection.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Aluminum Propeller Inspection”, PDF p. 307
notes.evidence: A transverse crack or flaw of any size is cause for rejection.

notes.front: An aluminium blade has three small, well-separated leading-edge nicks, all within repair limits. Is their number alone cause for rejection?
notes.back: D) No; a reasonable number of repairs may be made unless they form a continuous line that weakens the blade
notes.choices:
A) No, but the blade must be shortened
B) Yes; more than one injury always means rejection
C) Yes, if any is on the leading edge
D) No; a reasonable number of repairs may be made unless they form a continuous line that weakens the blade
notes.choicesExplained: B) The circular says more than one injury is not sufficient cause alone. C) Leading-edge nicks can be rounded out. A) Shortening is for tip damage.
notes.explanation: The concern is repairs lining up so they materially weaken the blade.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 8-73, p. 8-37
notes.evidence: More than one injury is not sufficient cause alone for rejection of a blade. A reasonable number of repairs per blade may be made and not necessarily result in a dangerous condition unless their location with respect to each other is such to form a continuous line of repairs that would materially weaken the blade.

notes.front: A blade is bent after a ground strike, and the owner wants it partly straightened so it fits the shipping crate to the repair station. What is the right call?
notes.back: B) Never straighten it; ship it as it is
notes.choices:
A) Straighten it cold, then ship it
B) Never straighten it; ship it as it is
C) Straighten it only halfway
D) Heat and straighten it carefully
notes.choicesExplained: A) Even partial straightening is forbidden before shipment. D) Heated blades must be rejected. C) Partial straightening can hide damage.
notes.explanation: Straightening in the field can conceal damage and let an unairworthy propeller return to service.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 8-73c, p. 8-40
notes.evidence: Never straighten a damaged propeller. Even partial straightening of blades to permit shipment to a certificated propeller repair facility may result in hidden damage not being detected and an unairworthy propeller being returned to service.

notes.front: A repair-limit chart gives a 3 percent allowable width reduction at a station where the blade drawing's minimum width is 2.00 inches. What is the minimum width after repair?
notes.back: B) 1.94 inches
notes.choices:
A) 1.97 inches
B) 1.94 inches
C) 1.40 inches
D) 2.06 inches
notes.choicesExplained: A) 1.97 takes off 0.03 inch, which is 1.5 percent. C) 1.40 takes off 30 percent. D) A repair cannot increase width.
notes.explanation: The allowance is 3 percent of 2.00, or 0.06 inch, taken off the width.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 8-74b, p. 8-42
notes.evidence: (d) Step 4. Calculate the blade width repair allowable (∆w):

notes.front: Under part 43 Appendix A, which of these is a propeller major repair?
notes.back: C) Retipping a wood propeller
notes.choices:
A) Lubricating the hub
B) Cleaning the blades with solvent
C) Retipping a wood propeller
D) Coating the blades with engine oil
notes.choicesExplained: A) Lubrication is servicing, not a repair. B) Cleaning is servicing. D) An oil film after cleaning is servicing.
notes.explanation: Retipping of wood propellers is on the list of propeller major repairs.
notes.source: 14 CFR part 43 (eCFR, current), Appendix A
notes.evidence: (iv) Retipping of wood propellers.

notes.front: An aircraft vibrates only between about 2,100 and 2,250 rpm and is smooth elsewhere. What is the likely cause?
notes.back: C) A poor engine-propeller match
notes.choices:
A) A blade out of track
B) Static imbalance
C) A poor engine-propeller match
D) Blade shake
notes.choicesExplained: A) Track problems typically cause vibration across the whole rpm range. B) Balance problems likewise show throughout the range. D) Blade shake is not a source of vibration.
notes.explanation: Vibration limited to a narrow rpm band is not normally a propeller problem.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 8-109a, p. 8-51
notes.evidence: If a vibration occurs only at one particular rpm or within a limited rpm range (e.g., 2200–2350 rpm), the vibration is not normally a propeller problem but a problem with a poor engine/propeller match.

notes.front: With the engine at 1,300 rpm, the hub of a vibrating aircraft turns in a flat plane with no orbit. Where does the vibration probably come from?
notes.back: B) The engine
notes.choices:
A) The propeller blades
B) The engine
C) The propeller's balance weights
D) The spinner shims
notes.choicesExplained: A) A propeller cause would usually show as the hub swinging in an orbit. D) Spinner trouble shows as wobble. C) Balance weights are part of the propeller.
notes.explanation: No orbit at the hub points away from the propeller.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Vibration”, PDF p. 308
notes.evidence: If the propeller hub does not appear to rotate in an orbit, the difficulty is probably caused by engine vibration.

notes.front: During a tracking check, one blade tip passes 3/32 inch forward of where the opposite blade touched the block. What does this show?
notes.back: C) It is out of track; look for a bent blade or flange, or wrongly torqued bolts
notes.choices:
A) It shows static imbalance
B) It is within tolerance
C) It is out of track; look for a bent blade or flange, or wrongly torqued bolts
D) It shows the blade angle is correct
notes.choicesExplained: B) 3/32 inch is more than the 1/16-inch tolerance. A) Tracking shows relative blade position, not balance. D) Tracking does not measure blade angle.
notes.explanation: The difference exceeds 1/16 inch, so the propeller is out of track.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 8-108f, p. 8-51
notes.evidence: If the propeller is out-of-track, it may be due to one or more propeller blades being bent, a bent propeller flange, or propeller mounting bolts that are either over or under-torqued.

notes.front: Reading a universal propeller protractor, the vernier zero lies just past 17 on the degree scale, and the vernier line four spaces from its zero aligns best with a degree line. What is the blade angle?
notes.choicesExplained: A) Vernier spaces are tenths, not whole degrees. B) This ignores the vernier reading. D) The vernier adds to the degree reading.
notes.explanation: Each vernier space counts one tenth of a degree.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Universal Propeller Protractor”, PDF p. 310
notes.evidence: The number of tenths of a degree in the blade angle is given by the number of vernier scale spaces between the zero of the vernier scale and the vernier scale graduation line nearest to perfect alignment with a degree scale graduation line.

notes.front: A mechanic needs to mark the 30-inch station on a blade before measuring its angle. Which marking method is wrong?
notes.back: D) A metal scribe
notes.choices:
A) A felt-tipped pen
B) A non-scratching marker
C) Following the manufacturer's station data
D) A metal scribe
notes.choicesExplained: A) A felt-tipped pen leaves no scratch. C) Using the manufacturer's station is correct. B) A non-scratching marker leaves the surface intact.
notes.explanation: A scratch from a scribe is a stress concentrator that can lead to blade failure.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Checking & Adjusting Propeller Blade Angles”, PDF p. 309
notes.evidence: Do not use metal scribes or other sharply pointed instruments to mark the location of blade stations or make reference lines on propeller blades

notes.front: On the knife-edge stand a propeller shows a definite tendency to rotate, and its total weight already equals the allowable limit. What correction is allowed?
notes.back: B) Remove weight at acceptable locations
notes.choices:
A) Add permanent fixed weights
B) Remove weight at acceptable locations
C) Change one blade's angle
D) Accept it as balanced
notes.choicesExplained: A) Adding weight is for assemblies under the allowable limit. C) All blades must be at the same angle during the check. D) A tendency to rotate means it is not balanced.
notes.explanation: At the weight limit, the only allowed correction is removal of weight.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Static Balancing”, PDF p. 310
notes.evidence: The removal of weight at acceptable locations when the total weight of the propeller assembly or parts is equal to the allowable limit.

notes.front: An owner asks for dynamic balancing to cure vibration, but the engine has worn, loose parts. What should the mechanic expect?
notes.back: A) Balancing will not help; worn or loose parts make it impossible
notes.choices:
A) Balancing will not help; worn or loose parts make it impossible
B) Balancing will fix it if done twice
C) Balancing will fix the vibration anyway
D) Static balancing will fix it instead
notes.choicesExplained: C) Balancing cannot cure poor mechanical condition. B) Repeating the run does not change that. D) Static balancing addresses the propeller alone, not loose engine parts.
notes.explanation: Dynamic balancing only improves vibration from mass unbalance of the rotating parts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Dynamic Balancing”, PDF p. 311
notes.evidence: Balancing does not reduce the vibration level if the engine or aircraft is in poor mechanical condition. Defective, worn, or loose parts will make balancing impossible.

notes.front: A dynamically balanced propeller must come off for engine work and go back on afterwards. What should the mechanic do before removal?
notes.back: B) Mark hub and engine flange with matching felt-tipped pen marks
notes.choices:
A) Scribe a line across hub and flange
B) Mark hub and engine flange with matching felt-tipped pen marks
C) Remove all balance weights
D) Rebalance it statically
notes.choicesExplained: A) Scribing scratches parts, and the handbook specifies a felt-tipped pen only. C) Removing weights would undo the balancing. D) Static balancing is done at overhaul facilities.
notes.explanation: Matching marks restore the same orientation and prevent dynamic imbalance.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Removal”, PDF p. 312
notes.evidence: make an identifying mark (with a felt-tipped pen only) on the propeller hub and a matching mark on the engine flange to make sure of proper orientation during reinstallation to prevent dynamic imbalance.

notes.front: A mechanic lightly oils the propeller mounting nuts and studs so they run on smoothly before torquing. What does the handbook say?
notes.back: A) Mounting hardware must be clean and dry to prevent excessive flange preload
notes.choices:
A) Mounting hardware must be clean and dry to prevent excessive flange preload
B) Oil only the studs, not the nuts
C) That is correct practice
D) Use grease instead of oil
notes.choicesExplained: C) The handbook calls for dry hardware. B) No part of the hardware is to be lubricated. D) Grease is a lubricant too.
notes.explanation: Lubricated threads would give excessive preload at the same torque.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Installation”, PDF p. 313
notes.evidence: Caution: Mounting hardware must be clean and dry to prevent excessive preload of the mounting flange.

notes.front: An aircraft on the handbook's example lubrication schedule flies only about 30 hours a year. What calendar lubrication interval applies?
notes.back: B) 6 months
notes.choices:
A) 12 months
B) 6 months
C) 24 months
D) Only every 100 hours
notes.choicesExplained: A) 12 months is the normal limit for aircraft flown more. C) The example never lengthens the interval. D) At 30 hours a year the calendar limit comes first.
notes.explanation: Annual use well under 100 hours cuts the calendar interval to 6 months.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Lubrication”, PDF p. 314
notes.evidence: If annual operation is significantly less than 100 hours, calendar lubrication intervals should be reduced to 6 months.

notes.front: A pilot reports rpm swinging a little above and then below the set value in a steady cycle. What is this, and what should be checked?
notes.back: C) Hunting; have the governor, fuel control and synchrophaser checked
notes.choices:
A) Surging; replace the propeller
B) Overspeed; reset the tachometer
C) Hunting; have the governor, fuel control and synchrophaser checked
D) On-speed; nothing to do
notes.choicesExplained: A) Surging is a large change that settles after one or two occurrences. B) Overspeed is a single-direction state, not a cycle. D) A steady cycle is not on-speed.
notes.explanation: A cyclic swing either side of the desired speed is hunting.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Hunting & Surging”, PDF p. 316
notes.evidence: Hunting is characterized by a cyclic variation in engine speed above and below desired speed.

notes.front: In flight, a turboprop pilot increases fuel flow. How does the propeller absorb the extra turbine torque?
notes.back: A) It increases blade angle, holding rpm constant with more thrust
notes.choices:
A) It increases blade angle, holding rpm constant with more thrust
B) It lets rpm rise at the same blade angle
C) It goes into beta
D) It feathers
notes.choicesExplained: B) The propeller holds constant engine speed in flight. C) Beta is a ground range below flight idle. D) Feathering is for shutdown or failure.
notes.explanation: More fuel means more turbine energy and torque, which the propeller takes up with a larger angle.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Turboprop Engines & Propeller Control Systems”, PDF p. 317
notes.evidence: The propeller, in order to absorb the increased torque, increases blade angle, thus maintaining constant engine rpm with added thrust.

notes.front: A turboprop is taxiing in the beta range, and the pilot moves the power lever. What sets the blade angle?
notes.back: B) The power lever position
notes.choices:
A) The propeller governor
B) The power lever position
C) The synchrophaser
D) The autofeather system
notes.choicesExplained: A) In beta the governor does not govern blade angle. C) The synchrophaser matches rpm in cruise. D) Autofeather is for power loss in takeoff and landing phases.
notes.explanation: In beta the power lever controls blade angle directly.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Turboprop Engines & Propeller Control Systems”, PDF p. 317
notes.evidence: In the beta range of the throttle quadrant, the propeller blade angle is not governed by the propeller governor but is controlled by the power lever position.

notes.front: A turboprop's propeller is giving zero thrust while the aircraft is being manoeuvred on the ground. Which operating range is this?
notes.back: B) Beta range
notes.choices:
A) Alpha range
B) Beta range
C) Feather
D) Governing range
notes.choicesExplained: A) Alpha is the flight range. C) Feather is for a stopped or failed engine. D) The governing range is about the speeder spring's rpm span.
notes.explanation: Zero or negative thrust for ground handling belongs to the beta range.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Turbo-Propeller Assembly”, PDF p. 317
notes.evidence: For ground handling and reversing (beta range), the propeller can be operated to provide either zero or negative thrust.

notes.front: At low power on the Hartzell turboprop system described, the blades reach the angle where the beta linkage moves the beta valve forward. What happens?
notes.back: A) Oil supply to the propeller stops, so the blades go no lower
notes.choices:
A) Oil supply to the propeller stops, so the blades go no lower
B) The blades feather
C) The blades go into reverse
D) The governor speeds up
notes.choicesExplained: B) Feathering needs oil to be dumped, not stopped. C) Reverse needs the power lever moved back. D) The governor setting does not change.
notes.explanation: The beta valve holds the blades at the primary blade angle, the minimum for flight.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Pratt & Whitney PT6 Hartzell Propeller System”, PDF p. 318
notes.evidence: Forward movement of the beta valve stops the oil supply to the propeller. This prevents the blade angles from going any lower.

notes.front: On the Hartzell turboprop system described, the pilot adds power in flight and the power turbine starts to speed up. What happens in the governor?
notes.back: D) The flyweights go overspeed, oil to the dome is restricted, and the feathering spring increases pitch
notes.choices:
A) The flyweights go underspeed and more oil enters the dome
B) Nothing; the governor ignores power changes
C) The beta valve reverses the blades
D) The flyweights go overspeed, oil to the dome is restricted, and the feathering spring increases pitch
notes.choicesExplained: A) Rising speed gives an overspeed, not an underspeed. C) Beta and reverse are power-lever ranges on the ground. B) The governor is what holds the selected speed.
notes.explanation: Higher pitch absorbs the added power and keeps the selected speed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Pratt & Whitney PT6 Hartzell Propeller System”, PDF p. 318
notes.evidence: The flyweights in the CSU sense this acceleration and the flyweights go into an overspeed condition because of the increase centrifugal force. This force causes the control valve to move up and restrict oil flow to the propeller dome.

notes.front: After fitting a new governor, a ground run-up at takeoff throttle gives 50 rpm more than the manufacturer's takeoff rpm. What should the mechanic do?
notes.back: A) Reset the adjustable stop on the governor until the prescribed rpm is obtained
notes.choices:
A) Reset the adjustable stop on the governor until the prescribed rpm is obtained
B) Accept it; more rpm means more thrust
C) Change the propeller's blade angle by twisting
D) Adjust the tachometer to read correctly
notes.choicesExplained: B) The prescribed takeoff rpm is the target, not more. C) Twisting blades is a repair station job and is not the governor setting. D) Adjusting the gauge hides the problem.
notes.explanation: The adjustable stop sets the maximum engine speed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Setting the Propeller Governor”, PDF p. 327
notes.evidence: reset the adjustable stop on the governor until the prescribed rpm is obtained.

notes.front: An engine delivers 200 brake horsepower to its propeller, and the propeller turns out 170 thrust horsepower. What is the propeller efficiency?
notes.back: C) 85 percent
notes.choices:
A) 70 percent
B) 118 percent
C) 85 percent
D) 30 percent
notes.choicesExplained: A) 70 percent would need 140 thrust horsepower. B) Efficiency over 100 percent would mean getting out more than goes in. D) 30 percent is not the ratio of the two figures.
notes.explanation: Efficiency is useful power out over power in: 170 ÷ 200 = 0.85.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Aerodynamic Process”, PDF p. 288
notes.evidence: Since the efficiency of any machine is the ratio of the useful power output to the power input, propeller efficiency is the ratio of thrust horsepower to brake horsepower.

notes.front: In flight, a blade section's chord lies at 20° to the plane of rotation and at 3° to the relative wind. Which figure is its angle of attack?
notes.choicesExplained: A) 20° is the blade angle, measured from the plane of rotation. D) Adding the two angles has no meaning. C) 17° is the angle between the relative wind and the plane of rotation, not the angle of attack.
notes.explanation: Angle of attack is measured between the relative wind and the chord.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Aerodynamic Factors”, PDF p. 290
notes.evidence: A = angle of attack (angle formed by relative wind and chord) B = pitch or blade angle

notes.front: How does a controllable-pitch propeller differ from a constant-speed propeller?
notes.back: The pilot changes controllable pitch directly; a governor changes constant-speed pitch automatically to hold rpm.
notes.explanation: The governor is the step that turned controllable-pitch into constant-speed propellers.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Controllable-Pitch Propeller”, PDF p. 293
notes.evidence: This type of propeller is not to be confused with a constantspeed propeller. With the controllable-pitch type, the blade angle can be changed in flight, but the pilot must change the propeller blade angle directly.

notes.front: Why are pusher propellers on land aircraft more prone to damage than tractors?
notes.back: Ground clearance is usually smaller, and the wheels throw rocks, gravel and small objects into them.
notes.explanation: A tractor sits ahead of the structure, away from what the wheels throw up.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Pusher Propellers”, PDF p. 292
notes.evidence: On land aircraft, where propeller-to-ground clearance usually is less than propeller-to-water clearance of watercraft, pusher propellers are subject to more damage than tractor propellers. Rocks, gravel, and small objects dislodged by the wheels are quite often thrown or drawn into a pusher propeller.

notes.front: How does one nonfeathering aluminium-hub Hartzell model differ from most in its use of governor oil?
notes.back: Its governor oil moves the blades to high pitch; on most models, oil gives low pitch.
notes.explanation: On that model, centrifugal twisting moment is left to move the blades to low pitch.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Hartzell Constant-Speed, Nonfeathering”, PDF p. 300
notes.evidence: One model of nonfeathering aluminum hub constant-speed propeller utilizes oil pressure from a governor to move the blades into high pitch (reduced rpm).

notes.front: Why has fluid anti-icing given way to electric deicing on modern aircraft?
notes.back: Fluid systems add weight, and their anti-ice time is limited by the fluid carried.
notes.explanation: Electric systems need no on-board fluid supply to run out.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Anti-Icing Systems”, PDF p. 304
notes.evidence: disadvantages in that it requires several components that add weight to the aircraft, and the time of anti-ice available is limited to the amount of fluid on board. This system is not used on modern aircraft, giving way to the electric deicing systems.

notes.front: How does synchrophasing go further than synchronisation?
notes.back: Synchronisation matches engine rpm; synchrophasing also holds a set angular relationship between master and slave propellers.
notes.explanation: Matching rpm removes the beat; matching phase goes on to reduce cabin noise.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Synchronization & Synchrophasing”, PDF p. 305
notes.evidence: Synchronization systems provide a means of controlling and synchronizing engine rpm. Synchronization reduces vibration and eliminates the unpleasant beat produced by unsynchronized propeller operation. The synchrophasing system is designed to maintain a preset angular relationship between the designated master propeller and the slave propellers.

notes.front: What is the difference between static and dynamic propeller unbalance?
notes.back: Static: the centre of gravity is off the axis of rotation. Dynamic: similar elements' centres of gravity are not in the same plane.
notes.explanation: Static is about where the mass sits round the axis; dynamic is about which plane it turns in.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Propeller Balancing”, PDF p. 310
notes.evidence: Propeller static imbalance occurs when the center of gravity (CG) of the propeller does not coincide with the axis of rotation. Dynamic unbalance results when the CG of similar propeller elements, such as blades or flyweights, does not follow in the same plane of rotation.

notes.front: How does surging differ from hunting?
notes.back: Surging is a large rise or fall in speed that returns to set speed after one or two occurrences; hunting keeps cycling.
notes.explanation: Both are speed variations; what differs is size and whether they settle.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Hunting & Surging”, PDF p. 316
notes.evidence: Hunting is characterized by a cyclic variation in engine speed above and below desired speed. Surging is characterized by a large increase/decrease in engine speed, followed by a return to set speed after one or two occurrences.

notes.front: How does a turboprop produce thrust compared with a turbofan?
notes.back: Indirectly: its turbine gives torque to a propeller, which gives most of the push; a turbofan produces thrust directly.
notes.explanation: The propeller is the main thrust producer on a turboprop.

notes.front: How does the beta range differ from the alpha range of a turbo-propeller?
notes.back: Alpha covers flight, using engine power at any flight condition; beta covers ground handling and reversing, with zero or negative thrust.
notes.explanation: The split mirrors the handbook's flight and ground types of control.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), Chapter 7, “Turbo-Propeller Assembly”, PDF p. 317
notes.evidence: The turbo-propeller provides an efficient and flexible means of using the power of the engine at any condition in flight (alpha range). [Figure 7-47] For ground handling and reversing (beta range), the propeller can be operated to provide either zero or negative thrust.
